A 21-year-old man was sentenced to seven years in prison in the United Kingdom on Monday after a string of cyberattacks targeting major companies including Grand Theft Auto VI maker Rockstar Games.

Arion Kurtaj, who was released on licence after already having spent years in custody, pleaded guilty last Monday to a series of hacking attacks that he carried out between 2021 and 2022 as part of the Lapsus$ hacking group.

"You are obviously a very talented young man," the judge said.

"Don't waste those talents by spending the rest of your life in and out of prison," he continued, adding that the sentencing decision required "balancing the seriousness of what you did with, on the other hand, your young age" and medical diagnoses.

Prosecutors said Kurtaj had caused "serious disruption to major international business" and put sensitive information at risk with the hacks.

In one incident, Kurtaj managed to obtain 90 gameplay videos from Rockstar's much anticipated and at the time unfinished GTA VI game before leaking them online under the pseudonym "TeaPotUberHacker." He also threatened to release the game’s source code, according to prosecutors.

Kurtaj is said to have used just a mobile phone, a hotel TV’s Wi-Fi and an Amazon Firestick to carry out the hack.

He also targeted neobank Revolut and ride-hailing firm Uber.

Kurtaj was initially arrested in September 2022 but was deemed not fit to stand trial following a medical assessment.

In 2023, he was handed an indefinite restricted hospital order. A court ruled in January 2026 that the hospital order could be lifted, and his case was scheduled for trial.

Iran flogged pop singer Parastoo Ahmadi and four members of her concert team on Monday following a December 2024 performance near Qom in which she sang without a hijab, her lawyer said.

Lawyer Mostafa Nili told Emtedad news channel that the Qom prosecutor's office enforcement team carried out the sentence against Ahmadi in the early hours of Monday.

A criminal court in Qom province had sentenced nine members of the concert team to 74 lashes each, a two-year ban on leaving the country and a two-year ban on artistic activity.

The judiciary also sealed off the Deyr Gachin Caravanserai, the historic venue where the concert took place.

'Hypothetical concert'

Ahmadi performed at the caravanserai near the historic city of Qom on the evening of 11 December 2024 without hijab. No audience was present.

The concert was broadcast live on YouTube and drew around 3 million views in the days that followed.

Ahmadi described the performance as a "hypothetical concert." Writing on her YouTube channel, she said, "I want to sing for the people I love. This is a right that I could not give up, that is, singing for the land that I love passionately."

The criminal court of Qom charged the group with "offending public decency by producing and disseminating vulgar and immoral content online."

Amnesty International called in June for the sentences to be quashed, saying flogging was "a cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment" that violated the absolute prohibition on torture and other ill-treatment.

The organisation called on Tehran to abolish compulsory veiling and corporal punishment and to end the criminalisation of freedom of expression.

Under Islamic Republic law, women are banned from singing in public in spaces where men are present.

Although criminal law does not explicitly criminalise women's singing as such, female performers typically face charges of encouraging corruption and prostitution, failing to observe hijab, or offending public decency.

Authorities have used the charge in recent years to close many Instagram pages belonging to Iranian female singers. Appearing in public without hijab is punishable by between 10 days and two months in prison, up to 74 lashes or a fine.

The sentences against Ahmadi and her collaborators stand in contrast to scenes from pro-government rallies held during the US and Israeli military strikes on Iran earlier in 2026, when images circulated widely showing women at the gatherings without mandatory hijab.

A performance by Lebanese singer Julia Boutros was also broadcast at a pro-government gathering in Tehran, where Boutros also did not wear hijab.

Earlier, during the Woman, Life, Freedom protest movement in 2022, Ahmadi had performed the protest song "Az khun-e javanan-e vatan" or "From the blood of the nation's youths".

After it was widely shared on social media, her home was searched by security forces and she was ordered to report to the security prosecutor's office in Tehran.

The Woman, Life, Freedom movement emerged in Iran in September 2022 following the death of Mahsa Amini, 21, in the custody of Tehran's morality police. Amini had been detained over alleged issues with her hijab.

Human rights organisations say the subsequent crackdown left more than 500 people dead.

The agreement builds on a 1951 defence agreement and comes after months of heightened tensions between Washington and the island under Danish sovereignty.

A new deal sealed in September and ratified by Denmark last week is boosting Washington's military presence in Greenland, while also giving it the right to block strategic investments by non-NATO and non-EU countries.

At the same time, it also explicitly reaffirms the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenlanders' right to self-determination.

What does the US get out of this deal?

The US already operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, an important site for missile warning and space surveillance.

But the new agreement lets Washington expand activities there and establish two additional defence areas: Narsarsuaq in the south and Mestersvig in the east.

It's also meant to give US aircraft broad overflight and landing rights across the island and provide access for Washington’s vessels in its territorial waters.

On top of that, it includes the possible deployment of Trump's proposed Golden Dome missile-defence system.

Troop numbers, construction budgets or deployment dates haven't yet been defined.

For Greenland, the agreement brings potential economic benefits, but also tighter security restrictions.

The US commits to awarding contracts for building and maintaining military facilities to Greenlandic companies as far as possible. That could create jobs and business opportunities.

What does the deal mean for the EU?

The EU is not a party to the agreement, and Greenland's status as an Overseas Country and Territory remains unchanged.

But the deal has important strategic and economic implications for Europe.

First, the investment restrictions could help limit Chinese and Russian influence over critical infrastructure and natural resources in the Arctic.

European investors are not excluded by the agreement. The EU already has a raw-materials partnership with Greenland, and the European Commission announced a separate 200-million-euro investment package in September covering areas including connectivity, energy and critical raw materials. But there is a strategic trade-off.

The agreement reinforces a US-centred security framework in the Arctic. And the EU has no formal role in deciding the island's new American military arrangements.

Does the agreement give US ownership over minerals?

The deal also restricts certain foreign investments in sensitive sectors, including critical infrastructure and natural resources.

“Big investments, there shouldn't be a backdrop for China to get into having a part in big mining projects", Rasmus Leander Nielsen, Associate Professor at the University of Greenland, told Euronews.

"But that de facto has been the case for several years already. So it's not something completely new."

Greenland must implement these rules in cooperation with Denmark, whose authorities will consult Washington on investment decisions. The aim is to limit potentially hostile foreign influence, particularly from countries outside the Western alliance.

For Greenland, however, this could narrow the pool of investors available to develop its economy and natural resources.

The agreement does not give the US ownership of Greenland's minerals or ban all non-Western investment. But it gives Washington a more formal role over certain foreign investments on the island.

Cost of living crisis: Is taxing the rich the way to go?

Also in today's episode, we look at growing calls across Europe to tax the wealthiest people more, as protests continue across the continent over the cost of living.

According to Eurobarometer, around two-thirds of Europeans back this approach. However, in most countries, popular support struggles to turn into concrete legislative action. Take Belgium, where fraught budget talks are ongoing to tackle the deficit.

As part of this, the coalition, made up of centre, left and right-wing parties, clashed after two parties demanded the rich help fill the gap.

This left-right divide also caused a political crisis in the Netherlands this month.

In Europe, countries like Switzerland, Norway and Spain already impose annual net wealth taxes. They generate between 0.2% and 1% of GDP, so the value is often difficult to quantify.

Economists warn that these measures can also discourage investments as well as increase the risk of tax avoidance.

"A net worth tax will probably not get you a lot of money and it will cost you growth. That's something that I see as very dangerous in Europe at the moment. In an economic environment that is very weak in general," told Euronews Dr Michael Christl, Research Fellow at Tax Foundation Europe.

What are the alternatives?

Another avenue is focussing on housing wealth. Britain, for example, will add an annual surcharge on homes worth over £2 million from 2028.

VAT reforms are also part of the conversation, but some experts warn that higher VAT hurts lower- and middle-income households most, since they spend a bigger share of their income on consumption. 

And under current EU VAT rules, countries cannot introduce a higher VAT rate exclusively for luxury goods.

No single tax ticks every box, so the answer may lie in a mix of smaller reforms.

But as the political crises in Belgium and the Netherlands over this debate show, agreeing on which ones is the hard part.

Academia neagă că ar fi transmis un punct de vedere despre Bălvăniș 

Numai că Academia Română nu a emis niciodată un punct de vedere pe această temă, reiese dintr-un răspuns remis PressOne de către Biroul de Comunicare & PR al instituției. Mai mult, la Registratura Academiei Române nu a fost niciodată înregistrată o cerere din partea AUR sau a unor persoane afiliate AUR pe acest subiect.

Din limba maghiară sau germană, localitatea Bálványos/Bad Götzenburg s-ar traduce drept Băile Cetatea Idolilor. 

Cuvântul „bălvan” la rădăcina toponimului Bălvăniș?

În expunerea de motive care a însoțit legea, susținătorii AUR arătau că numele localității Balvanyos (pronunțat Balvanioş) este un „toponim redat doar într-o formă străină, amintind de cea maghiară, fără ca să existe o formă românească scrisă şi pronunțată conform normelor ortografice şi ortoepice stabilite de Academia Română”. „Forma actuală generează dificultăți de pronunțare a literei S ca Ș și a literei Y ca I”, mai spun inițiatorii. Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) on Monday welcomed a ruling by a court in The Hague, the Netherlands, that bars Chinese carmaker BYD from selling its Ti7 SUV in the European Union because it copies the Land Rover Defender too closely.

BYD said it would appeal.

"BYD strongly disagrees with today's judgment and will appeal it. The BYD Ti7 is the result of BYD's own independent design work and infringes none of JLR's rights," the company said in a statement.

Some wonder if the solving of the famous Riemann Hypothesis by Anthropic’s Claude model is the beginning of advanced super intelligence.

Anthropic’s announcement on Friday that its Claude artificial intelligence model had helped solve what many had called the ‘biggest maths problem of all time’ has been met by both awe and terror for what the future of AI has in store for humanity.

Anthropic researcher and mathematician Levent Alpöge used Claude to find a solution to the 167-year-old math problem known as the Riemann Hypothesis, one of six remaining unsolved Millennium Prize problems carrying a $1 million (€913,000) reward from the Clay Mathematics Institute.

First proposed in 1859, the hypothesis suggests that the seemingly random appearance of prime numbers — numbers divisible only by one and themselves — actually follows a hidden, strict pattern.

Solving the problem could eventually have enormous real-world consequences, by giving certainty to the way prime numbers are distributed, computer systems, for example, can run more quickly and leaner.

Alpöge worked with Claude for months, submitting a partial result in August. This is not the first time he has explored using AI to solve maths’ biggest problems.

In September, he submitted a partial result proof to the Navier-Stokes and Euler equations, which govern fluid dynamics.

The Anthropic researcher submitted both this and his latest proof to Lean, the open-source, interactive maths proof platform which automatically checks proofs.

The platform is designed to test mathematical proofs and allow independent checkers to verify them. Within 48 hours, MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland and the Lean FRO/ Mathlib Initiative checked the proof and found zero errors.

His released proof spans 17,374,215 lines of Lean code spread across 175,187 separate files, backed by an unpublished, AI-generated text draft exceeding 250,000 pages.

The sheer scale of it means that humans have not yet had time to fully comprehend it, and even Alpöge was in awe of the ability of AI to solve the problem.

"Claude began to leave me in awe" and "far outpaced me near the finish line," adding that "Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."

Reaction

Many mathematicians have welcomed the proof.

Hector Pasten of the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile called it “something like a Rosetta Stone” that completes a dictionary between previously disconnected branches of math.

Oxford University’s James Maynard called it “something to be celebrated” because mathematicians finally know why it is true.

Independent Italian mathematician Alessandro Masullo, who released an incomplete, traditional human-written proof on the exact same day after 12 years of solo work, said he refused to use AI because he didn't trust it.

Some had expected that AI would take much longer to solve the problem, such as Australian American mathematician Terence Tao who predicted in October that AI would solve the Riemann Hypothesis by 2050. One month later, he was wrong.

Meta’s AI Chief Alexandr Wang took to X on Sunday warning that the achievement marked “the beginning of a significant change” that could usher in a “handover of society to AI”, arguing machines will soon supersede human capacity in every field.

Elon Musk meanwhile also saw it as a defining moment in the developing AI. He responded on social media platform X, “Unequivocal super intelligence has arrived. Welcome to the Singularity.”

Others have argued that the sheer length and scale of the proof, coming in at 250,000 pages long, makes it almost unreadable to humans, raising philosophical questions about whether mathematical truth matters if humans cannot comprehend it.

AI critics including Gary Marcus and godfather of AI Yann LeCun have pointed out that AI did not solve the problem by itself, rather it required months of human guidance and open-source infrastructure developed by mathematicians to find the solution, dismissing the finding as more hype than proof of a super intelligence.

What does it mean for society?

The solving of Riemann’s Hypothesis sets a major precedent for how science will be done in the future. By pairing human intuition with AI to solve complicated problems to create genuinely new insights that would normally be beyond human capacity.

In mathematics, hundreds of theorems that previously began with the caveat “assuming the Riemann Hypothesis is true…” are now officially proven facts. In computer science, it also confirms that certain algorithms used to process large prime numbers will always run reliably at high speeds.

It could also remove the need for code that previously treated the hypothesis as a theory, meaning computer systems can be learner and more efficient.

What it does not do is break internet encryption. If anything, the proof helps cybersecurity confirm that certain fast algorithms used to test whether a massive number is prime are 100% reliable.

Russian banks, crypto, "shadow fleet", oil refineries, soldiers and athletes are all targeted in the latest sanctions package proposed by Brussels.

The European Commission has proposed a new round of economic sanctions against Russia as the country disregards calls for an energy ceasefire and continues its relentless attacks aimed at making Ukraine's winter unbearable.

The proposal, unveiled on Monday afternoon, comes amid intensifying efforts to advance the peace negotiations into a multilateral format involving Ukrainian, Russian, European and US officials, although Moscow has yet to commit to taking part.

If approved by member states, it will mark the 22nd sanctions package since February 2022. Brussels aims for a deal in December before the holiday break.

"We will continue to propose new sanctions until Russia shows genuine intent for lasting peace in Ukraine," Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a video statement.

"Our position is clear: we are giving Ukraine the strength to secure peace – and Russia every reason to choose it."

The new sanctions seek to remove an additional 60 Russian banks from the SWIFT system, crack down on the crypto platforms that Moscow uses to bypass restrictions, and prohibit European companies from repairing Russian energy facilities, particularly oil refineries, which Ukraine's long-range strikes have significantly impaired.

The proposal also targets over 70 vessels from the "shadow fleet" that Moscow employs to bypass the oil price cap, currently set at $44 per barrel.

More than 670 of these vessels have already been denied access to EU ports and services. The decrepit ships, which lack standard insurance and often sail under false flags, are considered a security and environmental threat.

Von der Leyen has revived a measure from the previous package that was left pending: an entry ban on Russian soldiers who have fought in Ukraine.

The first attempt in July fell short after France and Italy raised concernsabout the administrative burden and legal responsibility for consular services.

But a recent spike in hybrid attacks, many of them attributed to Russian services, has injected fresh energy into the issue. Denmark has asked for tighter visa rules after foiling a Russian plot to assassinate a US-Ukrainian rapper on Danish soil.

"Russian ex-combatants pose a security risk to Europe. They cannot be allowed to wander freely across our countries," von der Leyen said.

"Therefore, entry into the European Union will be off limits."

The package introduces a novel dimension: sports and culture.

The Commission wants to exclude Russian teams and athletes competing under the Russian flag and the display of official Russian symbols from all sports events inside the bloc. It also wants to prohibit Russians from providing financial donations to and holding posts in governing bodies of European-based sports federations.

In July, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) lifted its suspension on Russian athletes ahead of the 2028 LA Olympics, triggering an outcry across Europe.

"Sports events can not be a forum for propaganda activities," von der Leyen said.

Notably absent from the Commission’s proposal is alumina, a key raw material used in aluminium production.

The issue came to prominence earlier this year after a media consortium exposed the links between Aughinish Alumina, a sprawling refinery in western Ireland, and Russia's military-industrial complex. Dublin came under intense pressure from Kyiv to cease the exports and was forced to launch a government probe.

The investigation reached no definitive conclusion because it did not find evidence to either confirm or refute a direct link between Irish-made alumina and Russian weapons.

Though publicly Dublin has said it would not "cherry-pick" EU sanctions, Brussels did not sense enough Irish support to move ahead with restrictions.

Monday's proposal is the first since the Commission established a sanctions office within its Secretary General, bringing together officials from different departments

Lars Danielsson, a veteran Swedish diplomat, has been appointed to replace David O'Sullivan as EU sanctions envoy. O'Sullivan spent the last few years travelling around the world, with a focus on Central Asia, to convince other countries to put pressure on companies that help Moscow bypass sanctions and buy blacklisted items.

China, in particular, remains a headache for Commission officials, dismissing their pleas. The country has become the central passage for circumventing sanctions, providing Moscow an essential lifeline to sustain its resource-intensive war.

"Every time we have a summit with China, we raise this issue," a senior official said.

Ahead of the presentation, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on allies to tighten sanctions on the components that Russia uses to build the jet-powered drones that terrorise the civilian population.

"International sanctions, enforcement of sanctions regimes, and genuinely tougher export controls are what can curb Russia's weapons production. Every country and every leader who helps pressure the aggressor also helps protect lives," he said.

Zelenskyy is set to attend a special EU summit later this week in Brussels.

Shares in Iceland's Blue Lagoon fell below their offer price when they started trading on Friday. The geothermal spa operator raised 14.3 billion Icelandic krónur (€104mn) in the country's first IPO in nearly three years.

Blue Lagoon, which runs Iceland's famous geothermal spa, saw its shares drop below their initial public offering price on Friday.

The company raised 14.3 billion Icelandic krónur (€104mn) in Iceland's first IPO in nearly three years. The previous one was by fishing company Ísfélag in December 2023.

Its shares opened at 85 krónur, 10.5% below the offer price of 95 krónur a share, and closed at 87.4 krónur, down 8%.

On Monday, the shares were trading slightly lower at around 86.3 krónur.

Listed under the ticker BLUE, Blue Lagoon is the 28th company on the main market of Nasdaq Iceland, the country's stock exchange.

Magnús Harðarson, president of Nasdaq Iceland, said in a statement that the listing gives investors access to a part of the Icelandic economy that has not been represented on the market before.

Blue Lagoon sold 150 million new shares, equivalent to 14.6% of the company after the offering.

The offering drew nearly 4,000 subscriptions, worth about 15.3bn krónur (€112mn), according to the company. That was roughly 7% more than the value of the shares on offer. About 40% of the shares went to individuals and 60% to professional investors and companies.

At the offer price, Blue Lagoon was valued at about 97.4bn krónur (€710mn), based on the 1.02bn shares it now has in issue.

Blue Lagoon began preparing for a listing in 2022 and had hoped to go public in 2023.

More than a lagoon

The company was set up in 1992 to research the lagoon's geothermal seawater. The lagoon lies in a lava field on the Reykjanes Peninsula in south-west Iceland.

The company now runs The Retreat and Silica hotels by the lagoon, the Michelin-starred Moss restaurant and two hotels in Iceland's highlands. It also sells skincare products abroad.

Its revenue reached a record €156mn last year, according to its offering documents.

Blue Lagoon is also buying Arctic Adventures, an Icelandic tour operator.

Including the tour operator, the company has budgeted revenue of €291mn for 2027. On its own, Blue Lagoon expects revenue of about €173mn this year.

It wants to use the IPO proceeds to develop new destinations, strengthen its balance sheet and fund growth.

One risk for the business is that the lagoon sits near Grindavík, a town that has been hit by a series of volcanic eruptions since late 2023.

The company said volcanic activity forced the lagoon to close for 49 days in 2023 and 76 days in 2024, but for only two days in 2025.

Tourism accounted for 8.8% of Iceland's economic output in 2025, up from 8.2% the year before, according to preliminary figures from Statistics Iceland, the national statistics office.

Blue Lagoon has said it expects to complete the Arctic Adventures deal at the end of November, when it will issue about 246 million new shares to the tour operator's owners.

They will then hold about 19% of the enlarged company.

South Korea’s education minister has resigned after criticism of last-minute changes meant to stop students from cheating by using AI on the country’s university entrance exam.

President Lee Jae-myung accepted Choi Kyo-jin’s resignation on Sunday, three days after the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), known locally as Suneung. Choi acknowledged that the government had failed to prepare adequately and that sudden changes had caused confusion.

On Monday, the Education Ministry said it was filing criminal complaints against five candidates caught using smart devices during the exam. Some complaints had already been filed, with the remaining cases due to follow by the end of the day, an official told Yonhap news agency.

Concern grew after the top scorer in this year’s certified tax accountant examination admitted on 15 November to cheating with a miniature camera, a smartphone and generative AI.

The confession came days before the university entrance exam, which plays a major role in students’ university choices and career prospects.

The Education Ministry had also reported four cases involving AI-enabled smart glasses in middle and high school exams this year.

Authorities deployed about 8,400 additional staff for the university entrance exam, including specialists checking for smart devices and monitors patrolling corridors. Supervisors were told to inspect students’ glasses and cover clothing buttons with stickers to block hidden cameras.

During the exam, the government sent three nationwide emergency alerts to mobile phones to detect devices that candidates had not handed over.

The ministry reported 111 suspected breaches involving electronic devices. Of those, 54 were detected through the alerts and 52 through other methods, while five involved candidates actually using smart devices. The figures do not establish that all 111 cases involved AI-assisted cheating.

Last-minute changes draw criticism

The government announced the additional staff two days before the exam. Teachers’ organisations questioned whether supervisors could learn to identify sophisticated devices at such short notice.

The Korean Federation of Teachers’ Associations criticised a timetable that left staff being selected on Tuesday, trained on Wednesday and deployed on Thursday.

The day before the exam, the ministry also restricted students to black pencils. Exam centres were to provide other supplies, including erasers and correction tape, to prevent candidates from hiding cameras inside them.

Choi had already drawn criticism for telling a parliamentary hearing on 16 November that his age made him doubt his ability to detect all AI-assisted cheating.

“Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation,” he said in his resignation statement.

Lee has put Prime Minister Han Seong-sook in charge of follow-up measures and ordered a review of how examinations are managed.

One proposal under consideration would add identification marks to question papers, allowing authorities to trace where photographed or leaked questions came from.

Bolt’s CEO spoke to Euronews about the company’s future IPO plans, why he believes Europe is falling behind, and whether the US could offer a more attractive market. He also shared his vision for the future of autonomous vehicles.

At just 27 years old, Markus Villig became Europe’s youngest self-made billionaire, thanks to Bolt, the mobility company he founded at the age of 19 in Estonia.

Now generating an annual turnover of more than €2 billion, Bolt’s founder and CEO, Markus Villig, said he knew the company was going to be a big success almost immediately.

“Honestly, after the first 30 days, it was very clear that this product resonates. Customers love it. They get access to more affordable and great transportation, drivers see that they're able to make more income than what they used to do, and it just took off immediately.”

Markus joined Angela Barnes in the studio for the latest episode of The Big Question to discuss the company’s future, the latest technological developments coming to Europe and Bolt’s IPO plans.

How soon will we see robotaxis in Europe?

While Bolt started its life as a ride-hailing taxi app, under the names mTakso and Taxify, it has since diversified into e-scooters, e-bikes, food delivery and courier services.

And the company’s next big move is robotaxis – self-driving vehicles that are expected to help bridge the gap between supply and demand, while reducing road traffic accidents.

“The technology is ready today,” Markus told The Big Question.

“When we look at what's going on in the US or China, robotaxis today are serving hundreds of thousands of passengers every single week. So this is no longer a fictional technology, this is something that works in the real world. And yet, at the same time, there's zero robotaxis operating in Europe at the moment.”

According to Markus, a combination of factors is holding back the bloc: a lack of domestic technology, regulation blocking adoption and fragmented regulation making widespread roll-out even more complex.

“Today in the European Union there's not a single advanced self-driving car company who could produce this technology domestically,” he criticised.

As a result, Bolt has had to look elsewhere.

Bolt has signed a deal with US electric vehicle maker Lucid to provide a 25,000-strong fleet, equipped with technology from Chinese company Pony.ai, for roll-out across Europe. Pilot programmes are expected to start within the next year.

Will Bolt IPO in Europe?

In short, no – not in the current climate. But that’s not because Markus doesn’t want to.

“As a European, I'd like to list in Europe. However, when I am looking at this neutrally as a CEO, I look at the facts.

“It's very clear that Europe is just very far behind in terms of access to capital. Today, it just clearly is not as attractive,” he told Euronews.

However, he is in no rush to take the company public, choosing to focus first on delivering its robotaxis and winning in that category. Markus also seemed optimistic that the situation in Europe could be fixed, hopefully by the time he’s ready to hit the stock exchange.

“If we really wanted to, we could reform the European capital markets. We absolutely have the funding we need, but we just need to structure it better so it would actually be competitive versus just going and listing in New York.

“There's absolutely potential to fix that, but we must do that urgently,” Markus added.

Other major artists who have joined the movement include Lorde, IDLES, Wednesday, Amyl & The Sniffers, Wolf Alice, Paramore, Rina Sawayama, Primal Scream, Soccer Mommy, Shygirl, Lucy Dacus, MJ Lenderman, MØ and AURORA.

The plant will be LEGO’s fourth in Europe, alongside its factories in Denmark, Hungary and Czechia.

The 115,000-square-metre factory will sit on a 60-hectare site, roughly the size of 120 football pitches. It will be less than half the size of LEGO’s Nyíregyháza factory in Hungary by building area. The new plant will mould and process bricks and pack finished sets.

Rasmussen said it would be LEGO’s most automated factory. “This new factory will be our most automated and advanced site, using innovative technologies to enhance productivity, sustainability and operational resilience.”

Portugal’s prime minister, Luís Montenegro, attended the launch in Estarreja on Monday. He said the government would work to make the land available and speed up construction so the jobs could be created as soon as possible.

Zagreb is demanding a settlement over a strategically important peninsula as Montenegro races to conclude its EU accession talks by the end of the year, raising fears that the dispute could derail its membership ambitions.

Croatia is stepping up diplomatic pressure on Montenegro to settle a territorial dispute as the candidate country races to conclude its EU accession talks, two diplomatic sources told Euronews on condition of anonymity.

Zagreb has a list of grievances dating back to the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s that it wants Podgorica to resolve before joining the EU. But in recent days, the Croatian government has intensified its demands over a long-running border dispute.

The diplomats say Croatia's real objective is to settle ownership of the Prevlaka peninsula and the surrounding territorial waters, with one dismissing its other demands as "smokescreens".

The other grievances, which Podgorica has already partly addressed, include locating the remains of prisoners of war, compensating Croatian families whose property was expropriated and returning a naval training ship that was in Montenegro when Yugoslavia dissolved in 1991.

"When it comes to the border issues, if we don't find any kind of solution that is for Montenegro and Croatia acceptable, then we can go to an international court or international arbitration. We are not against this kind of mechanism," European Affairs Minister Maida Gorčević told reporters last week.

Zagreb has so far resisted international arbitration. Instead, it wants Podgorica to recognise the findings of the Badinter Commission, established by the European Community in 1991 to provide legal opinions on the dissolution of Yugoslavia.

The commission established the principle that the boundaries between the former Yugoslav republics should become international borders upon independence. Croatia is now demanding that Montenegro formally recognise the existing land border.

On land, Prevlaka is little more than a virtually uninhabited strip of rock. But its strategic location makes it crucial to determining the maritime boundary between the two countries, with implications for navigation, access to the Bay of Kotor and potentially valuable offshore oil and gas reserves.

Since 2002, the two countries have coexisted peacefully under a temporary arrangement, with Croatia controlling the peninsula and Montenegro most of the surrounding waters.

Zagreb is now pressing Podgorica to reach an agreement by December, just as Montenegro is trying to conclude its EU accession negotiations before the end of the year.

Croatia leveraging its membership

Montenegro still has eight of its 33 negotiating chapters left to provisionally close. At an intergovernmental conference on Thursday, Podgorica had hoped to close at least four, but managed only two because of Croatian opposition.

Time is running out for the Western Balkan country to complete negotiations by the end of the year. That would probably require another intergovernmental conference before the end of November, followed by a final meeting in December.

Montenegro is the frontrunner to join the bloc and hopes to become its 28th member by 2028. But the bilateral negotiations are deeply unequal, with Zagreb effectively holding the keys to Podgorica's European future.

"If Montenegrin citizens feel pressured to make territorial concessions, it is the whole EU integration process that would be damaged in terms of public perception. The risk is that Montenegro enters the EU with a growing anti-European sentiment," the second diplomat said.

Germany has also urged Croatia, through the so-called Berlin Process, not to allow bilateral disputes to derail Montenegro's accession, particularly as the EU seeks to use enlargement to strengthen its influence in its immediate neighbourhood.

But the border dispute has become politically sensitive in Zagreb, where the government is eager to demonstrate that it is defending Croatian interests amid reports that it is considering calling early parliamentary elections in 2027.

"Before Montenegro concludes its EU accession negotiations, we want to reach an agreement on the land border. It is crucial that we establish whether the current Montenegrin government understands and recognises this fundamental principle, which is key to the post-1991 settlement," Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković told MPs earlier this month.

Croatia itself has an unresolved border dispute with Slovenia, which did not prevent it from becoming the EU's most recent member in 2013. Zagreb subsequently rejected an international arbitration ruling on the dispute in 2017.

The European Commission has said Montenegro has met the targets to provisionally close all 33 negotiating chapters, and it is now up to all 27 member states to unanimously green light their closure.

As so often in EU enlargement, political considerations have overtaken technical progress.

South Korean entertainment companies have faced barriers in China since a dispute over a US missile defence system in 2016. New trade commitments could improve access, but content checks on films remain and a return of K-pop concerts is not guaranteed.

South Korea and China have largely completed talks to expand their free trade agreement, with new commitments covering entertainment, tourism, and financial services.

The announcement came last week during talks between South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen.

Technical details, translations, and legal reviews still need to be completed before the expanded agreement can be formally signed, China's commerce ministry said.

China has agreed to treat film and video game businesses from South Korea the same as companies from other countries. It has also promised not to discriminate against Korean films and online games when reviewing them for approval, said the trade ministry in Seoul.

The agreement would expand joint production arrangements beyond films to include television dramas, animation, entertainment programmes, and documentaries. Productions officially recognised under these deals would qualify as Chinese content and so would not count towards quotas on foreign productions.

Films would still have to pass China's content review process before being released in cinemas, a South Korean official told The Korea Herald.

K-pop concerts remain uncertain

South Korean entertainment has faced restrictions in China since Seoul's decision to deploy a US missile defence system in 2016. Beijing has never formally acknowledged the restrictions, which have affected films, television programmes, and live performances.

A senior South Korean presidential official said the agreement did not require either country to approve concerts, but had opened more channels for discussion with Beijing, The Korea Herald reported.

Industry representatives remained cautious about whether the commitments would lead to practical changes.

"We will have to see whether practical measures that affect the content industry follow," an official at a South Korean drama production company told Yonhap News Agency.

South Korean tour operators established in 23 designated areas of China, including Beijing and Shanghai, would be allowed to arrange overseas trips for Chinese citizens and foreigners living there.

In return, South Korea has agreed to expand access for Chinese companies in legal, retail, and audiovisual services. Both countries have also agreed not to require technology transfers as a condition of investment.

China's commerce ministry described the agreement as a joint effort to oppose protectionism and support international trade.

Disruptions to oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran war have pushed Asian countries to look at larger emergency reserves, shared storage, and closer cooperation with fuel suppliers as shortages squeeze their economies.

Japan has launched a regional task force to help Asian countries build up emergency oil reserves and plan joint responses to shortages, as the Iran war interrupts supplies from the Gulf.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi announced the initiative on Tuesday at the Asia Zero Emission Community leaders' meeting in Manila, held alongside the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit. A joint statement by Japan and the International Energy Agency (IEA) confirmed that the task force had been established.

Tokyo also proposed using unused oil storage tanks, including those at closed refineries, to hold reserves for other Asian countries. This would create shared oil storage across the region.

Around a quarter of the world's seaborne oil trade passed through the Strait of Hormuz in 2025, with about 80% of those shipments heading to Asia, according to the IEA.

The task force will work with the IEA and the Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia to assess oil reserves and explore how countries could coordinate their response to shortages.

Japan and the IEA also outlined plans for an oil security centre in Tokyo, supported by the agency's teams in Paris and Singapore. It would help countries develop storage systems, share information on oil markets, and prepare for emergencies.

"We would like to position this as an Asian version of the IEA," Takaichi said.

The energy body coordinates emergency oil releases among its members. Oil-importing countries such as Japan must hold stocks equivalent to at least 90 days of net oil imports.

Countries in the IEAagreed on 11 March to make 400 million barrels from their emergency reserves available to the market in response to the Iran war, the largest coordinated release in the agency's history.

Plans for shared oil storage

Singapore, Indonesia, and Malaysia have expressed support for the storage proposal, Cristina Roque, the trade secretary from the Philippines, said on Monday.

The United Arab Emirates has also shown interest in storing oil in countries with available facilities, she added.

However, arrangements allowing countries to draw on one another's reserves have yet to be agreed.

Japan and the Philippines also signed a three-year agreement on Monday to help Manila develop its own emergency oil reserves, which covers cooperation on storage facilities, financing and rules for managing and releasing supplies.

Takaichi also outlined a separate proposal for closer cooperation between Middle Eastern oil producers and Asian consumers. Japan wants to help connect the two regions and strengthen their energy supplies, its foreign ministry said.

The European Commission on Monday opened a formal antitrust investigation into Coca-Cola Europacific Partners (CCEP), the largest supplier of fizzy drinks in eight EU countries. It suspects the company abused its dominant position to stop retailers buying across borders.

"People across Europe enjoy soft drinks every day. But they should not have to pay more simply because they live in one EU country rather than another," said Teresa Ribera, the Commission's executive vice-president for clean, just and competitive transition, who oversees competition policy.

"We are investigating whether Coca-Cola has been putting barriers between national markets, making it harder for retailers to buy products across borders and secure better deals," she said.

CCEP is headquartered in the UK and is one of the two largest European bottlers of Coca-Cola brands. It sells those drinks, along with other brands, in Belgium, France, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden.

The Commission is concerned that CCEP may have abused its dominant position in the wholesale supply of carbonated soft drinks and sports drinks to supermarkets and other retailers. Restaurants, hotels and cafés are not part of the case.

The investigation will look at whether CCEP:

  • made wholesale price cuts conditional on drinks not being exported to other EU countries
  • sold different packaging volumes in different countries to restrict cross-border trade
  • gave retailers incentives to limit imports of fizzy drinks into Spain
  • refused to let retailers negotiate deals covering several countries at once, insisting instead on separate national negotiations

"This could undermine the Single Market, limit competition and ultimately mean higher prices and less choice for consumers," Ribera said.

If proven, the practices could breach Article 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU, which bans companies from abusing a dominant position. Here the alleged abuse is dividing the Single Market along national borders.

The investigation comes three days after an EU-UK summit in Brussels, Belgium, where UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham sought to show he is delivering the closer post-Brexit ties promised by his predecessor, Keir Starmer.

Because the Commission has opened proceedings, national competition authorities can no longer apply EU competition rules to the same practices.

Researchers will test whether an AI tool helps radiologists detect breast cancer.

Researchers in the United Kingdom will test whether artificial intelligence tools can help improve breast cancer detection, in the world’s largest study of its kind.

Early breast cancer detection can save lives, but diagnosis can be a time-consuming process. Currently in the UK, at least two radiologists review every mammogram, or breast x-ray, but very few — less than 1% — of these scans actually show signs of cancer.

In the trial, known as EDITH, radiologists will use an AI-assisted tool to help detect cancers that are too small to see or feel. The goal is to give specialists more time to diagnose and care for women with cancer, while reducing the time they spend reviewing mammograms with no signs of disease.

“If successful, this technology could help women get a breast cancer diagnosis and start treatment much more quickly, giving them the best possible chance of recovery,” said Yvette Cooper, the UK’s health and social care secretary. The UK government is backing the trial with £10 million (about €12 million).

The study will enroll about 660,000 women aged 50 to 71 who are due for a routine breast cancer screening, which is offered every three years in the UK. Women can opt out if they do not want to take part in the trial.

Women will be split into three groups: the first group will undergo a standard breast cancer screening, with two radiologists reviewing the x-rays. In the second group, a radiologist and the AI tool will both review the mammograms to see if the AI tool catches any signs of cancer the radiologist may have missed.

In the third group, the AI tool will take the first look at an x-ray and determine whether the likelihood of cancer is high or low. If it is low, one radiologist will review the images, but if it is high, two radiologists will check the images and decide whether to refer the patient for additional testing.

The AI tool could “help experts review images more efficiently,” said Fiona Gilbert, a radiology professor at the University of Cambridge and one of the study’s lead researchers. She is also studying whether AI can help identify women at higher risk of developing breast cancer.

Every mammogram will still be reviewed by at least one radiologist, according to the trial announcement, and the AI-assisted tool will only be integrated into routine breast cancer screening if the study shows it is as safe and effective as the existing screening programme.

Currently, around 2.1 million women in the UK undergo breast screening each year, preventing around 1,300 deaths.

Breast cancer is the most common form of cancer in the European Union, with an estimated 360,000 women diagnosed in 2024, EU data shows. That accounts for 29% of all cancer diagnoses in women.

Since 1995, UN climate and environment summits have often seen deadlock, delays and frustration.

The COP31 climate negotiations in Antalya have ended without a final deal. The EU and other countries rejected a cover decision because it did not cover how to quite fossil fuels or fund climate action in developing countries.

As the COP process depends almost 200 countries reaching a consensus, it is far from easy, especially with geopolitical tensions as they are.

Since the first United Nations' Conference of the Parties (COP) in 1995, many summits have seen fierce arguments when countries failed to find common ground.

Here we take a look back at previous COP summits where tensions ran high.

2000: COP6, The Hague

At COP6 in 2000, held in The Hague, the negotiations were suspended. Talks resumed months later in Bonn, where the secretariat of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change is based.

The summit took place at a time when the United States was locked in an extremely tight presidential election. Negotiators did not know whether the next leader of the world's largest economy would be George W. Bush, who was sceptical of climate policies, or Al Gore, who would later share the Nobel Peace Prize for his climate advocacy.

Ironically, Bush's election victory, and his subsequent rejection of the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, encouraged other countries at the resumed Bonn talks to push ahead with plans to implement the protocol.

However, France's former chief negotiator Paul Watkinson criticised the summit, saying it ended in "chaos".

2009: COP15, Copenhagen

Expectations rose after the election of US President Barack Obama. But COP15 failed to deliver the binding global climate agreement many countries had hoped for.

Deep divisions between developed and developing countries, especially disputes between Washington and Beijing, blocked a deal on mandatory cuts in emissions.

In the end, the conference only agreed to "take note" of the non-binding Copenhagen Accord. The accord included a goal of keeping the rise in global temperatures below 2 degrees and a pledge by rich countries to provide 100 billion dollars a year in climate finance by 2020.

2012: COP18, Doha

Countries agreed a second commitment period under the Kyoto Protocol. But major emitters such as the United States, Russia and Canada did not take part.

Critics of the deal argued that the targets were not ambitious enough and that the arrangement covered an ever-shrinking share of global emissions.

2019: COP25, Madrid

Talks in Madrid overran their scheduled finish time by more than 40 hours, as they did this year at the summit in Antalya.

At COP25, countries failed to agree rules to govern international carbon markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

The summit's final text disappointed the countries most vulnerable to climate change and environmental groups, because it did not include a significant increase in emissions reduction pledges.

2022: COP27, Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt

Countries agreed to establish a historic "loss and damage" fund to support those most affected by climate change.

But negotiators were unable to strengthen commitments to phase down the use of fossil fuels. Many governments and climate activists criticised the outcome, arguing that there had been insufficient progress on cutting emissions.

2024: COP29, Baku, Azerbaijan

At COP29 rows over climate finance for developing countries pushed the negotiations beyond their planned end date.

Negotiators struggled to bridge differences over the scale of financial commitments between rich and poor nations.

The summit eventually produced an agreement, avoiding a complete breakdown. But many developing countries judged the outcome to be inadequate.

Antimicrobial resistance is a health security threat. Europe can lead global action

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global threat that no country can tackle alone.¹ World AMR Awareness Week, from 18 to 24 November, puts this shared responsibility into focus: countries must work together to preserve effective medicines and support the development of new treatments.

AMR raises the risk of serious complications and death from common infections. It is already putting pressure on health systems across the world.¹ Europe can play a key role in the global response to this issue, but only if the European Union (EU) and national governments implement effective support and rewards for antimicrobial innovation alongside existing stewardship policies. This article draws on discussions at a GSK-hosted educational AMR workshop at the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases (ESCMID) conference earlier this year and includes expert insights from:

· Florian Wagenlehner, Director, Clinic of Urology, Paediatric Urology and Andrology, Justus Liebig University, Giessen, Germany

· Jorge Mestre-Ferrandiz, Associate Professor, Charles III University of Madrid, Spain

· Matteo Bassetti, Director, Infectious Diseases Unit, AOM – IRCCS San Martino Polyclinic Hospital and Department of Health Sciences (DISSAL), University of Genoa, Italy

AMR is not tomorrow’s problem

AMR occurs when microbes, including bacteria and fungi, evolve to resist medicines designed to treat them, known as antimicrobials.¹ Globally, it is directly responsible for more than one million deaths each year and roughly €61 billion in direct healthcare costs.¹ ′ ² In Europe alone, the annual toll exceeds 35,000 lives and costs health systems around €11.7 billion.³ ′ ⁴

Europe is not on track to meet four of the five AMR targets set by the EU Council for 2030.⁵ These include ambitions to reduce overall antibiotic use, increase the proportion of prescribed antibiotics made up of first-choice “Access” antibiotics, and cut bloodstream infections caused by three major resistant bacteria.⁵ Failure to meet these targets will make it harder to reach the United Nations’ goal of reducing global AMR-related deaths by 10% by the same year.⁶ Without intervention, the burden of AMR on patients, healthcare systems and society will continue to grow.⁷

"For a patient, AMR becomes real when an antimicrobial does not work as expected," says Wagenlehner. "That can mean more complex treatment, more uncertainty and more time before we get the infection under control. When effective treatment options are limited or delayed, resistant infections can become life-threatening."

Responsible use matters – but new medicines are also needed

Misuse and overuse of antimicrobials remain the main drivers of AMR.¹ The more frequently microbes are exposed to antimicrobials, the greater the likelihood that resistance will develop.¹ This is why stewardship policies and practices that promote the careful and appropriate use of antimicrobials to slow down resistance are essential.

"Stewardship balances providing patients with the antimicrobials they need, while avoiding unnecessary use that would drive resistance," Wagenlehner explains. "For example, antibiotics are one type of anti-infective. They treat bacterial infections, not others such as viral ones, and using them when they are not needed can drive resistance."

However, stewardship alone is not enough. Europe also needs new antimicrobial options if it is to stay ahead of evolving resistance. These priorities are complementary; effective stewardship preserves today’s medicines, while innovation ensures we continue to stay ahead of resistance.

Why are we not getting enough new treatment options?

Since 2017, 17 new antimicrobials have been authorised globally, with only two of these representing new classes of antimicrobials.⁸ This means few new and differentiated treatments are coming forward.⁸ ′ ⁹ Innovation is therefore not keeping pace with the rise in drug resistance observed in microbes that cause infections, and we are not sufficiently addressing the diversity of ways in which microbes continue to outsmart the treatments that we have today.⁵

"When an infection becomes resistant to an antimicrobial, we need new medicines with diverse ways of overcoming that resistance," says Bassetti.

One of the main reasons resistance continues to outpace innovation is the increasingly challenging economics of antimicrobial research and development (R&D), exacerbated by ineffective funding models for antimicrobials once they become available.¹⁰ ′ ¹¹

The combination of high R&D costs and strong, appropriate stewardship creates a financial barrier to investment in innovative antimicrobials.¹⁰ ′ ¹¹ Traditional pharmaceutical business models rely on recouping R&D costs through sales volumes, yet novel antimicrobials are designed to be used sparingly to slow the development of resistance, creating a fundamental mismatch.¹⁰ ′ ¹¹

"Unlike medicines for common diseases, new antimicrobials are often held in reserve or used as a last resort, so companies may never recoup their R&D costs," says Mestre-Ferrandiz. "That is why many developers have stepped back from antimicrobial research, and why new economic incentives are needed."

Alongside the financial disincentive, health technology assessments (HTA) – the formal process used by health authorities to evaluate the value and costeffectiveness of new medicines and inform pricing and reimbursement decisions¹² – often fail to capture the full societal value of antimicrobials.¹³ This includes the readiness and resilience they bring to health systems and can lead to them being undervalued.¹³

"Innovative antimicrobials offer the best chance of getting ahead of resistance, rather than relying on variations of existing medicines," says Mestre-Ferrandiz. "Part of the value of a new antimicrobial is knowing there are additional options to treat infections if they become resistant to existing treatments."

Today, fewer developers are investing in antimicrobial R&D, resulting in a smaller group of new antimicrobials currently being researched or developed, with too few and insufficiently diverse products reaching the market.⁸ ’ ¹¹ Without intervention, this trend will only continue.

A new way of valuing antimicrobials is emerging

Governments are increasingly recognising this market failure and introducing "pull incentives", mechanisms that reward developers for bringing antimicrobials to market.¹¹ Some models delink financial returns from sales volumes, incentivising successful innovation regardless of how much of a product is sold.¹¹ “Appropriately funded pull incentives that delink payment from volume (i.e., payments independent of sales volume) and HTA processes that comprehensively assess the true societal value of antimicrobials are likely to be the most effective,” argues Mestre-Ferrandiz.

The UK's subscription model is the clearest example; it pays a fixed fee linked to National Health Service (NHS) value rather than volume, explicitly supporting stewardship and predictable supply.¹⁴This makes an antimicrobial available for use in the country, even if clinicians use it sparingly. This is a global first,¹⁴ but other countries have followed suit; Sweden has piloted a partially delinked revenue-guarantee model that rewards companies for keeping antibiotics of particular medical value available and ready for delivery.¹⁵

"Rewarding availability and clinical and societal value, rather than utilisation, can provide the predictability developers need without creating pressure to oversell antimicrobials that should be used responsibly," says Mestre-Ferrandiz.

Elsewhere in Europe, other forms of pull incentives have been implemented. Italy has created a €100 million fund to support development of, and access to, new innovative antimicrobials,¹⁶ while Germany has introduced a “reserve” antibiotic pathway that exempts qualifying products from part of the standard benefit-assessment process.¹⁷

The EU has signalled its intention to coordinate region-wide policies in a similar direction.¹⁸ This is an important step to support countries across the region in creating sustainable environments for antimicrobial innovation.

"A few promising examples do not yet add up to a stable system," cautions Bassetti. "The issue now is scaling these to create a sustainable market for antimicrobials across Europe."

Fair share: why European coordination matters

There is growing consensus amongst experts: delinked, value-based national pull incentives should be funded at fair share levels, an approach where countries contribute funding in proportion to the size of their economies.¹⁹ In 2019, analysts estimated $310 million (US) in global annual revenue, per priority antibiotic, across 10 years would be needed to support continued antibiotic R&D, helping bring more new and more diverse antimicrobials to patients.¹⁹ Splitting the financial commitment in proportion to the national gross domestic products (GDPs) of G7 and EU27 countries, a “fair share” approach, would spread costs and stabilise the market.¹⁹ However, currently only the UK and Italy are likely to meet their fair share targets.¹⁹

"Fair share is ultimately about solving the collective action problem," says Bassetti. "Broad participation, proportionate to economic capacity, is how you build a durable global system that supports innovation, supply resilience and access."

Every country benefits from new antimicrobials, but if only a few establish sufficient incentives, it will not be enough to increase R&D investment and will limit new options coming onto the market.¹¹ ’ ¹⁹

The next steps for Europe

Europe has an opportunity to drive the AMR response by setting a clear direction to implement solutions at scale across countries. The EU has already made this a political priority,¹⁸ but real change will only be realised if this is accompanied by national action.

This is an opportunity for European finance and health ministers to come together and look at AMR as an imminent threat to health security and economic stability.²⁰ ’ ²¹ Appropriate pull incentives can respond to the distinctive economics of AMR: antimicrobials require substantial investment to develop but must be used sparingly to preserve their effectiveness.¹⁰ ’ ¹¹ By rewarding value and availability rather than sales volume, these incentives can help reverse declining investment in antimicrobial R&D and support the development of effective new treatments for patients now and in the future.¹¹

"Europe already has the policy tools, scientific base and some early country examples," says Mestre-Ferrandiz. "The challenge is turning those pieces into a system for sustained progress."

World AMR Awareness Week is an opportunity to turn awareness into coordinated action that rewards antimicrobial value, promotes stewardship and strengthens health security and resilience. With 2030 targets approaching, Europe needs cross-sector collaboration to urgently address the growing burden of AMR.⁶

India has offered Nepal a development cooperation package worth 240 billion Nepali rupees (€1.4 billion) to help it recover from the catastrophic floods that tore through the Himalayan country in August.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi made the announcement in New Delhi, India, on Monday, standing alongside his Nepali counterpart Balendra Shah.

A disaster on a vast scale

The 26 August disaster began with a chain of events high in the Himalayas. A glacial collapse sent large amounts of rock, ice and meltwater into valleys below, triggering powerful floods downstream.

The resulting surge of water and debris entered rivers that flow through valleys in Tibet and Nepal, causing them to rise rapidly.

Floodwaters swept away homes, buildings, roads and bridges and carried mud and rocks downstream.

Disinformation, cyberattacks and the geopolitical use of migration put Spain in the sights of foreign powers. Experts urge shielding key sectors and speeding a joint European response to election interference.

In recent months, and especially throughout 2026, Europe has experienced an unprecedented escalation of hybrid attacks that have moved beyond the purely digital sphere to disrupt everyday services and critical infrastructure.

According to investigative journalists and European cybersecurity agencies such as the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA), in the last six months more than 50 physical incidents linked to foreign intelligence have been documented, in addition to thousands of cyberattacks.

Looking ahead to Spain's general elections on 29 November, which hybrid threats are causing most concern in these elections?

Carlos Galán Cordero, a professor at Nebrija University and an expert in hybrid threats, warns about disinformation.

"Spain is an attractive target for foreign powers. We know that Russia uses disinformation as its main tool, but there are other actors that resort to different tactics to influence elections or stir up the streets, provoking some kind of social unrest," he said.

The battle to influence the Spanish vote

Dealing with hybrid threats requires a response on several fronts. The most urgent task is to shield critical infrastructure and modernise IT systems in key sectors, from healthcare and food supply to electoral networks, backed up by greater intelligence sharing and rapid reaction teams at European level.

"There are many actors with a strong interest in seeing one candidate or another win," Galán Cordero says. Asked which countries or agents are seeking to disrupt the electoral process in Spain, he points to multiple foreign powers.

Although effective contingency plans are in place, as seen recently with a disinformation campaign detected by Maldita.es that had very limited impact and barely any reach, experts warn that there is no room for complacency, since these actors can update their methods in search of greater interference.

Europe's common strategy

The European Union has a common strategy that has been significantly tightened between 2024 and 2026 in response to the surge in sabotage, cyberattacks and electoral interference.

However, national security remains the responsibility of each member state, so the European model works more as a coordination network, a system of binding standards and information exchange than as a single agency.

Focusing only on Russia gives a skewed picture, since other countries operate in this arena through hybrid threats such as using the migration crisis to exert pressure.

"Migration can indeed be used as a means of creating instability," Galán Cordero continues.

Although the Spanish government maintains that there is no conclusive evidence to formally attribute the mass entry into Ceuta to Morocco, geopolitics experts point out that this is precisely how the so called "grey zone" works.

Pro-Moroccan networks coordinated during episodes such as the Ceuta crisis show how third powers exploit regional vulnerabilities to apply pressure without leaving an official trace.

"Not long ago someone sent me a meme showing Spain as a coveted and contested piece on the global chessboard, fought over by Washington, Beijing, Moscow, Rabat and Tel Aviv. The truth is that there is already a contingency plan under way that is detecting and neutralising these actions in time," Galán Cordero adds.

Brussels' legal and diplomatic arsenal

The European Union's joint response combines political action, infrastructure protection and digital control. To react quickly to hostile campaigns, Brussels has the Hybrid Toolbox (EU Hybrid Toolbox), which allows sanctions and joint responses to be coordinated, and the new Emergency Security Protocol proposed by Ursula von der Leyen in September 2026, inspired by Article 4 of NATO.

To protect critical infrastructure, the European framework already imposes specific obligations. Internally, the NIS2 and CER directives require strict cybersecurity and early warning standards in vital sectors such as energy, healthcare and food.

In the digital and electoral sphere, the Digital Services Act (DSA) and the European Democracy Shield monitor algorithm transparency and advertising on platforms such as TikTok or X.

All this is reinforced through cooperation with NATO, based on joint exercises and the Helsinki Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats.

When hybrid threats hit everyday life

It is also crucial to protect the information space by forcing digital platforms to provide genuine transparency about their algorithms and political funding, while strengthening media literacy among citizens so that disinformation become less effective.

The hybrid offensive in Europe is no longer an abstract threat; it is hitting everyday life and essential services head on.

In recent weeks the continent has seen a chain of incidents ranging from fake bomb threats on commercial flights and in schools to sophisticated digital sabotage against critical infrastructure, such as the cyberattacks suffered by several blood banks, which put at risk the preservation of vital reserves for transfusions and clinical trials.

This gap between technological speed and institutional response capacity defines today's information ecosystem.

In his book "La guerra: teoría para comprender los conflictos del siglo XXI" (War: A Theory for Understanding 21st-Century Conflicts) Spanish military officer Federico Aznar, an expert in disinformation and geopolitics, warns that "old solutions no longer work," and the new ones do not quite match the problems they are meant to address. That questioning of the current model is what underlies the idea of post truth."

Cybersecurity and monitoring to counter electoral falsehoods

With Spain's 29 November elections approaching, preventive measures combine the national security architecture with European cooperation, focusing on several key areas.

With the ballot in sight, Spain has activated its own preventive shield in line with Brussels. Under the coordination of the National Security Department and the Interior Ministry, bodies such as the National Cryptology Centre (CCN CERT) and INCIBE are working to secure the IT infrastructure of the electoral process, from data transmission networks to public information portals, against possible cyberattacks or impersonation attempts.

The digital investigation collective Antibot4Navalny, which tracks pro Russian disinformation campaigns, uncovered in November 2026 a coordinated offensive called Operation Matrioska, aimed at interfering in Spain's general elections.

The content pushed by this network seeks to discourage voting by alleging a supposed economic collapse caused by the housing crisis, calls for an end to sanctions on Russia and the withdrawal of funds from Ukraine, and promotes territorial fragmentation in Europe. The campaign circulates fake videos that mimic the look and style of media such as 'El País' and 'El Mundo' to lend credibility to disinformation narratives.

Fact checkers and citizens against electoral disinformation

The Monitor Disinfo association is dedicated to investigating, analysing and educating about disinformation and hybrid warfare. Carlos Galán Cordero is part of this association: "We analyse messages and campaigns on social media and share these issues with platforms such as Maldita.es, Newtral and similar organisations so that they can verify them."

Newtral has launched the FIMI Radar (Information Manipulation and Foreign Interference) to monitor foreign interference during the election campaign, while Maldita.es has highlighted its "Buloteca" archive ahead of 29N with the slogan 'Estas elecciones, la desinformación la frenamos juntos' - 'In these elections, we stop disinformation together'.

"This community is really good at helping to verify whether something is true or not," Galán Cordero continues. To stop these campaigns, he places the first line of defence with citizens, urging them to spot falsehoods and report them to the platforms themselves. Although there is a European legal framework to support this, such as the Digital Services Act (DSA), he warns that it will be in force for the 29N elections without yet having been rolled out with all the necessary effectiveness.

At the same time, intelligence services are keeping the digital ecosystem under surveillance to detect coordinated bot campaigns or narratives designed to sow doubts about the integrity of postal voting and the vote count.

Democratic resilience in the face of hybrid warfare and AI

This national deployment also draws on the European framework of the Digital Services Act (DSA), through which Spanish and EU authorities are demanding that platforms such as TikTok, X and Meta exercise greater control over their algorithms and political advertising during the final stretch of the campaign.

The aim is to prevent the scenario already seen elsewhere in Europe from being repeated in Spain: a combination of digital noise, falsehoods and sabotage designed to erode citizens' trust at the most sensitive moment for democracy.

Technological foresight and alliances to shield democracy

In this constantly evolving context, defending democracies means combining technological foresight with international cooperation. Professor Galán Cordero sums up the scale of the challenge like this: "Hostile actors have a lot of imagination when it comes to cyberattacks and are prepared to do whatever it takes to undermine the democratic values of Spain and Europe."

Facing campaigns increasingly driven by artificial intelligence, the expert highlights the preventive work of the National Cryptology Centre, which anticipates risks through constant simulations and testing, and stresses the need to act as part of a network: "We live in an increasingly globalised world and we need help from third countries to fight these threats. Spain is also an intelligence provider for allies that draw on our knowledge to tackle their own challenges."

In the face of a disinformation machine operating on an industrial scale through bot networks, troll farms and algorithms designed to fragment society, the response must be proactive.

Federico Aznar argues in his book that "technology reaches geopolitics" and that, in the era of post truth, "the main value to protect against these attacks is encapsulated in the integrity of society."

Nvidia vice president Rev Lebaredian also underlined the need for more energy:

"I believe it is essentially a failure of leadership to describe in a positive way the future that AI will bring," he said.

Many women work through their periods despite severe pain. One restaurateur from the Allgäu exempts affected female staff from duty. But how much consideration is appropriate at work?

When orders pile up in a restaurant, there is little time to catch your breath. For female employees with severe period pain, long hours on their feet, carrying heavy plates and working under time pressure in the kitchen and in service can be particularly hard.

At the Schlosskeller restaurant in Bad Hindelang in Bavaria they are not supposed to have to battle through their shift at any price. According to his own account, owner Peter Brutscher plans around their complaints when drawing up the rota.

On Instagram the restaurateur writes that for years he has deliberately taken female employees with severe period pain off the rota for two to four days, completely "without discussion".

Cramps, nausea or circulatory problems are physical limitations which, especially in the demanding hospitality sector, need to be taken seriously. His principle is: "The female cycle should not be ignored, but understood".

Not everyone has been understanding about this. "Of course I have been laughed at for it," Brutscher told the Allgäuer Zeitung. According to its report, his experience with one colleague prompted him to pay closer attention to such complaints when planning shifts.

How this consideration is organised is crucial, however. The magazine Focus reports that female employees can move shifts to another week. This does not automatically mean additional paid days off.

Many women work despite severe complaints

The fact that Brutscher is addressing a widespread problem is shown in a new study by the Institute for Employment Research (IAB), the research body of the Federal Employment Agency based in Nuremberg.

According to the study, 63% of the women surveyed feel limited in their daily work tasks by menstruation-related complaints, and 23% feel strongly limited.

For the study, a total of 2,107 women in dependent employment between 25-55 years of age were surveyed in spring 2026. They had all had their period in the previous six months.

According to the IAB, the weighted survey provides the first representative data on this topic for Germany.

The extent of the burden can hardly be read from days of absence alone. Only 13% had missed at least one full working day in the six-month period because of their complaints. Even among women who felt strongly impaired, 56% had no days off sick. Many therefore keep working even though they find their day-to-day tasks difficult.

In research this phenomenon is called presenteeism, which can go hand in hand with reduced concentration, resilience and productivity.
