A post shared by Peter Brutscher Gastro Consulting (@gastrogoat.peter)

Menstruation still a taboo

There is also the concern about being perceived differently at work. More than 80% of respondents reject the idea that women should hide menstrual complaints in the workplace. At the same time, 64% report doing exactly that. More than half believe women would be seen as less resilient if they spoke about it openly.

Flexible working hours, longer breaks or working from home can ease the burden for those affected, but these options are not available to everyone. According to the IAB survey, 45% can arrange their working hours flexibly, and 37% can work from home.

Women with severe complaints in particular often make use of these possibilities, provided their job offers them.

Working from home is not an option in kitchens and front-of-house service. Other forms of relief can help here, such as more flexible shifts. Similar approaches exist in care work: RTL Nord recently reported on the concept of the intensive care service "Kunterbunte Butterfliege" in Grasberg, Lower Saxony.

The organisation takes account of the cycle and complaints of its female employees if they wish. Such models require staff to be able to express their needs and for work to be organised dynamically within the team.

Researchers recommend more flexibility

Menstrual complaints should also be taken more into account when designing working conditions. This is the view of a team led by Eva Schultz from the Institute of Occupational, Social and Environmental Medicine at Goethe University Frankfurt. In their review "The influence of the menstrual cycle on everyday working life" the authors summarised the existing research.

They describe how cramps, back and headaches, fatigue or difficulty concentrating can impair work. Tabooing the subject and a lack of flexibility in the workplace make the situation even more difficult.

As possible forms of support, the team mentions flexible working hours, working from home and more education in the workplace. At the same time, the authors call for caution when assessing the existing research. Many findings are based on retrospective information from the women surveyed, without their complaints being checked by a doctor.

Which measures are particularly effective therefore still needs to be investigated.

Spain as a pioneer

While Brutscher relies on arrangements within the business, Spain has created special legal protection. Since 1 June 2023, women there can obtain a special sick note for menstrual complaints that make them unable to work. This requires a medical certificate, and the state covers the financial security. The common term "menstruation leave" is therefore misleading. What is meant is health-related absence, not extra days off for rest.

Portugal has since followed with a more narrowly defined rule. Since April 2025, employees with severe menstrual pain as a result of doctor-confirmed endometriosis or adenomyosis can take up to three consecutive days of paid leave per month.

Now Spain is even extending its approach to certain conditions associated with the menopause. From 1 December 2026, affected employees will be able to obtain a special sick note if a medically diagnosed condition temporarily makes it impossible for them to work. The menopause alone does not create an entitlement.

Consideration must not become a disadvantage

A statutory special rule and flexible rota planning like Brutscher’s in the Oberallgäu are different ways of dealing with health burdens.

A voluntary shift swap is not a substitute for a sick note. In Germany, the general rules on illness apply to incapacity for work due to menstrual complaints.

The question is therefore not only what kind of support a company offers, but also how naturally employees can use it. The IAB survey illustrates the obstacle: more than half of women fear that an open approach to menstrual complaints will be taken as a sign of lower resilience.

In his restaurant, Brutscher relies on explicitly acknowledging such complaints. But for an offer like this to really provide relief, trust is crucial above all. Those who accept support should not have to fear for their professional reputation.

With a new computing power centre, international collaborations and a robotics lab, the small South Caucasus country seeks to turn its technological talent into greater economic influence.

The ancient Silk Road carried goods, knowledge and ideas between East and West. In Armenia, tech industry leaders are re-imagining it in the modern day: a network linking countries through the infrastructure needed to develop artificial intelligence.

"What we are starting to rebuild is the ancient Silk Road," said Rev Lebaredian, vice president of NVIDIA responsible for physical AI simulation, speaking at the DigiTec Technology Conference in Yerevan. "It is coming back, but in this new form, as a kind of AI Silk Road," he said.

He argued that Armenia and Kazakhstan can become its main pillars, with countries in the region contributing at different levels of the AI economy: energy, microprocessors, computing infrastructure, models and applications.

The vision goes beyond constructing data centres. It is about connecting markets, researchers, businesses and capital across borders, and creating a role for smaller economies in an industry dominated by much larger powers.

"We must work hard to create as much interdependence between us as possible," Lebaredian said. "That will help everyone’s prosperity and strengthen our security."

The emerging corridor is starting to take physical shape.

Firebird, a US-based AI infrastructure company with Armenian co-founders, opened a computing centre in Armenia in August and is building another one in Kazakhstan.

With more than 6,100 NVIDIA Blackwell processors, the Armenian facility provides the computing power businesses need to train and run artificial intelligence systems. NVIDIA itself is among its clients, while Perplexity also collaborates with it, linking the small country with international AI players.

A small country looking beyond its borders

This ambition runs through the DigiTec Conference, held from 20 to 22 November at Yerevan’s Meridian Expo Center. The organisers announced 125 speakers, including representatives of NVIDIA, OpenAI, Dell Technologies and Mozilla, bringing international technology companies together with governments and entrepreneurs from the region.

For Armenia’s technology community, the event is also a space to showcase the position the country wants to secure.

Armen Kocharyan, president of the Union of Advanced Technology Enterprises UATE, which organises DigiTec, described it as a "live platform" that connects governments, investors and businesses from Europe, the Gulf, Central Asia and North America".

"A real hub never stops at borders. [...] We promote all five layers of artificial intelligence together, connecting people, technology, capital and markets in real time," Kocharyan said.

"We are creating a live platform" that brings together governments, investors and businesses from Europe, the Gulf, Central Asia and North America so they can develop technology, invest and expand their activities."

For a country of around three million people, these connections are essential. Armenia’s domestic market cannot by itself support the growth of an AI industry.

The opportunity lies in specialisation and cooperation with neighbours and partners, members of the Armenian technology community stress.

7% of national GDP

The political interest is also clear: the DigiTec programme includes a discussion between Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Nvidia's Lebaredian on turning the vision of an AI hub into reality.

The country is building on an already developed technology sector.

Arto Minasyan, co-founder of AI companies Krisp and 10Web and an investor in new technology ventures, said the sector makes up 7% of the Armenian economy, and described an ecosystem with its own unicorns, investment funds and research labs.

"The dream of building a technologically advanced Armenia pushed me to found the company and move from academic research into entrepreneurship," said Minasyan.

"It pushed my co-founder David to come back from Silicon Valley and start the company. It pushed many researchers from leading universities to come to Armenia and join forces to build here," he added.

This international network is a key element of the strategy. The Armenian diaspora provides connections through which know-how, information and business opportunities can flow.

The advice to build a supercomputer

The first tentative steps towards attracting Nvidia to Armenia also had a personal motivation. Lebaredian described how, after he set up Nvidia's office in Moscow in 2004, he began dreaming of something similar for Armenia, waiting for the right conditions to emerge.

The Armenian office opened in 2022. Today it employs more than 100 people, he says.

But attracting an international technology company was only one part of the ambition. The bigger question was how Armenian researchers and entrepreneurs would get the tools needed to develop technology themselves.

Lebaredian recounted a meeting at Nvidia's California headquarters in 2019, when Pashinyan asked the company’s co-founder Jensen Huang what Armenia should do to attract a company like Nvidia.

According to Lebaredian, the answer was to build an AI supercomputer for its people.

He said that initial efforts to secure state funding were halted by the pandemic and the war. The commercial project later took shape, as partners, capital and clients came together, with DigiTec 2024 serving as a meeting point.

This journey matters, because Armenia’s proposal relies on more than access to imported chips. The country has a tradition in computing dating back to the Soviet era, as well as expertise in semiconductor design and in the software used to develop them.

Armenia’s Minister of High-Tech Industry and Artificial Intelligence, David Tadevosyan, focused on the same challenge: how to turn successes in software and technology services into domestic research, engineering and production of internationally competitive products.

He highlighted human capital, modern infrastructure and cooperation between science and business as the necessary conditions.

The minister said the government had approved, around two weeks before DigiTec, an educational programme in physical artificial intelligence, involving international-level experts.

The aim, he explained, is for technological development to boost the productivity and competitiveness of the entire economy.

Firebird: The "AI factory" and expansion into Kazakhstan

Firebird’s facility in Hrazdan is the most visible expression of this strategy. An AI factory provides the computing power businesses need to train and run artificial intelligence systems, without having to build their own data centres.

Speaking to Euronews, Firebird co-founder and CEO Razmig Hovaghimian described a project that from the outset was driven by an ambition to go beyond the country’s borders.

"Why build it only in Armenia? Why not build it with Armenia as a starting point, expand it globally and attract talent and investment here?" he said.

An Armenian originally from Egypt with experience in creating and selling tech businesses, he saw in AI an opportunity to tap the country’s human capital.

Implementing it, however, required more than good engineers: funding, licences to export US technology and investors’ trust in a market they were not used to associating with such large-scale infrastructure.

"We knew we had the talent. We just had to convince the rest of the world that this is the right place to build and grow," he said.

According to Hovaghimian, the first phase has around 6,200 GPUs, while demand was for about 25,000.

"Everyone was saying that perhaps we would have one customer who would take all the capacity. We have 15," he said, adding that 12 of them are Armenian companies.

The customers he named include Nvidia and Perplexity, as well as Krisp and Activeloop. The presence of domestic firms shows that the facility can also serve as infrastructure for the local ecosystem, beyond serving international clients.

The second phase is already under construction, he said, with the aim of bringing the infrastructure in Armenia to around 70,000 GPUs in 2027.

"Today we are at 6,200. We are already building the second phase. Next year we will be at around 70,000," he told Euronews.

The expansion into Kazakhstan fits the same logic: developing infrastructure in markets that have talent and business potential but need access to AI computing power.

Hovaghimian put Firebird’s broader international plan at around two to two and a half gigawatts, with additional markets under exploration.

Firebird’s ambition, he stressed, is to give more countries the ability to develop their own technology.

"Not simply to become passive consumers of AI, but to take an active part in creating it."

An entire country as an AI laboratory

For Lebaredian, computing infrastructure is the starting point for the next step, "physical artificial intelligence" that involves robots, autonomous vehicles and systems that operate in the real world after being trained and tested in simulations.

He sees applications from agriculture and manufacturing to health and transport, sectors that account for a large part of the global economy.

In Armenia, a new robotics and physical intelligence lab links universities, the state and businesses to develop researchers and practical applications.

"To turn the whole country into our laboratory and our industries into a lab," he proposed, referring to mines, agriculture and high-tech production such as drones.

In his view, Armenia’s small size can make cooperation easier and speed up the move from research to deployment.

That is where the success of the new Silk Road will be decided: in the country’s ability to turn computing power into home-grown businesses and technologies.

In Europe, five cities made the top 10 for expats – including three in Spain.

Earlier this year, Panama was named by InterNations as the best country for expats in 2026.

Now, the global expat community platform has named its top cities for those moving abroad – and Ras Al Khaimah in the UAE has come out on top.

The ranking is based on a survey of 7,786 expats living around the globe who were quizzed on things like the friendliness of the local population and availability of online admin services.

Asked to rank their satisfaction in each category out of seven, these were then used to judge cities against indices including personal finance, ease of settling in, quality of life, expat essentials and working abroad.

Ras Al Khaimah came out on top for ease of settling in, working abroad, and expat essentials, and was second for personal finance. Of those polled, 84% of expats said they are happy with life in RAK, versus 70% globally. Nearly a quarter (24%) said they were very happy.

The city, which is around an hour’s drive north of Dubai, is growing in popularity thanks to its accessibility to nature, with an abundance of hiking trails as well as beaches nearby.

The emirate is also undergoing a transformation with an influx of luxury developments, with the UAE’s first casino resort set to open here in 2027.

The best European cities for expats

As for Europe, five cities made it into the top 10 – three of which are in Spain.

Málaga placed third, coming out number one for happiness, with 86% saying they are happy with their life, 42% of which are completely happy.

It’s no wonder then that 51% of those polled planned to stay forever, compared with just 27% globally.

The Andalusian city came out third for personal finance, with 73% of people rating the cost of living positively, while it also came fifth for quality of life.

Next up is Lisbon, which is regularly ranked among the top places to live abroad, placing sixth overall.

The Portuguese capital came out fifth on both the personal finance and ease of settling in indices, as well as 10th for quality of life.

Next up is Madrid, which was eighth, Valencia in ninth, and The Hague in the Netherlands rounding out the top 10.

Valencia was ranked first for quality of life, the fourth year in a row.

The German cities ranked poorly for housing, language, and digital life.

Ministerul Public a prezentat raportul la șase luni după ce procurorul general Cristina Chiriac a preluat mandatul. Astfel, între 15 aprilie și 15 octombrie 2026, procurorii din Parchetul de pe lângă Înalta Curte de Casație și Justiție și parchetele de pe lângă curțile de apel au soluționat 253.031 de dosare penale, în medie aproape unul pe minut.

Procurorii au trimis în judecată 29.813 persoane, au efectuat 5.084 de percheziții și au arestat preventiv 3.750 de persoane. Parchetul General transmite că prioritate au avut dosarele vechi – 26.655 de cauze mai vechi de cinci ani au fost soluționate.

Raportul prezintă deschis și problemele identificate, precum și ce își asumă instituția pentru următoarele șase luni.

Unde au contat cel mai mult rezultatele:

  • Banii statului. În dosarele de evaziune fiscală, prejudiciul estimat a fost de peste 403 milioane de lei, iar sechestrele au acoperit 58% din această sumă. În toate dosarele soluționate, bunurile puse sub sechestru depășesc 861 de milioane de lei.
  • Persoanele vulnerabile. Au fost înregistrate 12.242 de ordine de protecție, dintre care 84% confirmate de procuror. În dosarele cu autori și victime minore, 2.254 de persoane au fost trimise în judecată.
  • Femicidul. Au fost soluționate 45 de dosare de femicid, iar 29 de persoane au fost trimise în judecată.
  • Acțiuni coordonate. Operațiunea JUPITER 5, desfășurată în iunie împreună cu Poliția Română, a vizat 300 de dosare și 403 suspecți, cu măsuri asigurătorii de peste 141 de milioane de lei.

Ce nu merge încă:

  • Ministerul Public identifică cinci domenii în care rezultatele nu sunt cele propuse: combaterea corupției din magistratură, stocul încă ridicat de dosare, răspunsul judiciar în cazurile de violență împotriva femeilor, dotările tehnice și criminalistice și violența din școli.
  • Cea mai importantă măsură anunțată este o analiză la nivel național a tuturor soluțiilor de netrimitere în judecată din dosarele de violență împotriva femeilor, pentru a vedea unde au existat deficiențe, diferențe de practică între parchete și situații de risc evaluate greșit. Rezultatele vor fi prezentate în martie 2027.
  • Pentru școli, fiecare parchet va avea un procuror responsabil de cazurile grave de violență din mediul școlar, iar audierea elevilor victime se va face adaptat vârstei, pentru a nu-i expune unei noi traume. Ministerul Public va face și o situație la nivel național a acestor dosare, iar cauzele care întârzie nejustificat vor fi verificate.

Declarația procurorului general, Cristina Chiriac:

“Aceste cifre nu sunt nici un motiv de mândrie, nici o scuză. Sunt punctul de plecare. Vă arătăm unde suntem, ce merge, ce trebuie îmbunătățit sau reparat și unde trebuie să ajungem. Peste 250 de mii de dosare soluționate înseamnă enorm de multă muncă, dar stocul este încă mare, corupția din magistratură nu este investigată la nivelul pe care ni l-am propus, iar răspunsul nostru în cazurile de violență împotriva femeilor trebuie să fie mai rapid și mai eficient.

În spatele fiecărui dosar e un om care așteaptă un răspuns. Pentru el, contează mai puțin câte dosare am soluționat și mai mult dacă al lui a fost tratat corect și la timp. Încrederea în justiție nu se câștigă cu cifre mari, ci cu onestitate. De aceea am ales să spunem deschis și unde nu am reușit, și să ne asumăm public ce vom face până la următorul raport”.

Maritime Rescue and the Civil Guard have escorted five boats to La Restinga and located a sixth. The island is hosting nearly 900 migrants amid a record November.

Migration pressure on El Hierro, in Spain's Canary Islands, intensified again on Sunday with the arrival of around 300 migrants aboard five cayucos, the traditional wooden fishing boats used on the Atlantic route from West Africa. Authorities also located a sixth vessel in waters close to the island.

Spain's Maritime Rescue Service and the Civil Guard carried out the rescue operations and transferred the people to the port of La Restinga.

According to Spanish public broadcaster RTVE, the five boats that have arrived so far were carrying 74, 82, 22, 35 and 79 people respectively, among them around 20 minors. The Civil Guard patrol boat Río Tajo and the rescue vessel Diphda took part in the operations.

With these latest arrivals, around 900 migrants are now being housed in facilities on the island, whose reception capacity is under enormous pressure. Some of them are expected to be transferred to other islands in the Canary archipelago between Monday and Tuesday.

A historic November for the Canary route

The surge follows several days of mass arrivals that have overwhelmed the resources available on El Hierro, an island of barely 12,000 inhabitants. More than 2,500 migrants reached the Canary Islands between Saturday and Sunday. That is the highest number of rescues recorded in a single day in the 30-year history of the Canary migration route.

The European Union’s latest move is the AI Gigafactories initiative, which could mobilise over €30 billion in public and private investment to build large AI computing facilities.

Data centres are buildings filled with servers that store and process information behind everyday services, from online banking and hospitals to public transport and streaming. Having them closer to users can make digital services faster and more reliable, while making it easier to comply with European privacy laws.

Data centres also attract major investment in Europe's digital infrastructure and create short- and medium-term jobs.

But there is a catch. Data centres consume huge amounts of electricity, water and land. In Ireland, they accounted for 23% of metered electricity consumption in 2025, up from 5% in 2015. Some regions now restrict new connections because their grids cannot keep up. Cooling servers also requires water, particularly problematic in drought-prone areas.

Then there is the cost. In 2025, average industrial electricity prices in the EU were roughly twice those in the US, making European facilities more expensive to operate. Building them also requires land, power lines, fibre-optic cables and expensive cooling systems.

Unless electricity comes from low-carbon sources, expanding data centres can increase emissions. The challenge is finding enough energy, space and money to support growth without putting too much pressure on local communities and the environment.

As AI becomes increasingly embedded within travel, research weighs in on its potential, the challenges and whether travellers are willing to completely put their trust in the developing technology.

Could your holiday soon be planned, booked and managed by artificial intelligence (AI) agents and tools?

With the new technology increasingly finding its place in the travel industry, and becoming more sophisticated, more travellers are turning to it for advice. But questions remain about whether AI is able to meet the demand of growing expectations and how much travellers are willing to trust it.

Whether it’s a gap between the technology developing rapidly, yet being unable to impart accurate and complex information, or its development becoming pervasive, yet relegated to the background, to which extent are travellers willing to use it for planning?

Here’s what industry leaders and research predicts for AI and how it could influence the future of travel.

Amadeus: Why 2032 is seen as a ‘horizon year’

According to new research by Amadeus, 2032 will be a “horizon year” for the industry where AI will “transform travel”.

In its latest report, "The Intelligent Journey 2032", the global travel technology company explored, using scenarios, the uncertainties and challenges that may shape a model of travel futures.

Developed in collaboration with Stratforma, the research identified critical uncertainties that may lie ahead:

The great disconnect: In this scenario, travellers’ use of AI comes to a head when fragmented systems, geopolitics and physical-world failures “overwhelm” its capabilities – the technology is able to “handle travel inspiration and recommendations but still cannot reliably deliver complex travel”, Amadeus said.

As such, humans will still be the “frequent fallback” in instances where automation cannot coordinate the whole journey and for high-stakes events.

Balanced boundaries: Amadeus foresees AI becoming increasingly capable by 2032, yet, users will be “more deliberate” about when to use it.

“Technology moves into the background, removing unwanted friction while preserving the choice, discovery and human connection that make travel valuable,” the company said.

Despite becoming increasingly sophisticated and pervasive, Amadeus predicts that “digital separation” will become sought after in exchange for authenticity, privacy, serendipity and genuine human interaction.

Machine vs. machine: By 2032, travellers’ expectations are expected to rise amid the industry having successfully integrated AI at a systems level. Travellers will also believe they have the tools in place that will deliver on their expectations. However, disappointments won’t be seen as unavoidable and will instead be blamed on suppliers.

Further, as more decisions take place between machines, it will become more important to have transparency on how said decisions are reached.

Travellers served? The industry will also need to navigate showcasing the value of AI integration amid what Amadeus referred to as “widespread customer anxiety” about how the technology can provide services at an attractive price. As such, traveller adoption of the technology is likely to be “uneven and hesitant”.

Concerns, such as privacy, autonomy, fairness and accountability, will remain at the forefront of travellers minds, which the industry will have to create safeguards for.

IATA: Travellers using AI for planning

In its 2026 Global Passenger Survey, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) found that AI is becoming a more prominent tool for people’s travel plans.

With results based on more than 10,000 responses from 200 countries, 49% of travellers said they have used AI for their planning. This includes 21% who have used it to search for flights to a specific destination, while 19% say they used it to look for the cheapest flights. Lastly, 17% of respondents used it for their travel inspiration.

"People are using AI to plan their travel,” Nick Careen, Senior Vice President, Operations, Safety and Security at IATA, said. “It’s important for airlines not only to ensure their offerings show up in AI, but also to develop convenient links to convert an AI conversation into a real booking.”

Dnata: AI and the traveller experience

For the Group CEO of global aviation and travel services company dnata, AI has the potential to transform travel experiences.

Speaking to Euronews Travel at the 2026 Arabian Travel Market in Dubai, Nabil Sultan Al Murr said that the technology is already changing how holidays are planned and sold.

“I honestly think that AI and technology will bring in huge advantages in terms of improving the whole passenger experience and being able to put out the best offers and products,” he said.

TOURISE: AI use for inspiration, but not for decisions

The “Future Traveller” report by TOURISE and Euromonitor International, which looks into how changing priorities are reshaping global tourism, found that travellers are keen to use AI assistance, but remain independent when it comes to the final decision-making.

According to the report, 31% of travellers will use it for travel planning and booking in 2026. This is a trend especially pronounced among Millennial users, with 34% using it for travel planning and booking, compared to their Gen Z counterparts at 29%.

Meanwhile, 59% use AI for information or recommendations – a trend especially high among Gen X (65%) and Baby Boomers (67%), as well as Millennials (57%).

Beyond just a planning tool, the research also suggested that AI will shift to becoming a “travel companion”, with 64% of respondents surveyed in 2025 saying they would pay for an AI assistant to provide information during a trip.

Booking.com: Excitement alongside sceptic sentiment in Europe

Travellers aren’t so keen on relinquishing total control, however. In its Global AI Sentiment Report released in 2025, Booking.com found that only 12% of travellers would be comfortable having AI tools make decisions on its own. This highlights a “clear boundary when it comes to fully handing over control to automation”, Booking said.

Further, when it came to feelings of distrust towards the information generated by AI, North America ranked highest at 32%, followed by Europe and the Middle East at 29%.

The research drew on insights from 37,000 consumers across 33 markets. Despite the above scepticism, 86% of European and Middle Eastern respondents reported being excited by AI and its opportunities, while a further 74% were familiar with the technology and how it works.

Globally, however, 91% are excited about AI, yet just 6% “fully trust” it. Meanwhile, 10% feel “very uncomfortable” about the technology, “refusing to trust AI without human approval”.

That being said, 89% also said they want to use AI in their future travel plans – especially as more people (24%) found it to be a more trusted source in comparison to bloggers or social media influencers, at 19% and 14%, respectively.

“Generative AI represents one of the most significant technological shifts of our era, fundamentally reshaping how consumers engage with the world around them," said James Waters, Chief Business Officer at Booking.com.

Waters added that developments within the technology is also " raising the bar” for what they expect in terms of their evolving needs.

Aven Hospitality: Accuracy will decide who travellers trust

Ahead of the Phocuswright Conference held in November in Florida, industry leaders weighed in on how travellers will plan trips in 2027, and pointed to the importance of accuracy and the technology “proving itself” in instances where there are disruptions.

For Teresa Mackintosh, CEO at Aven Hospitality, which provides AI-powered hospitality software to properties, the technology hasn’t yet been able to bridge the gap between its systems and booking channel – putting hotels at a disadvantage.

“It's one thing for an AI assistant to recommend a hotel,” she said. “But quite another for it to find accurate rates and check availability in real time, then complete a booking.”

This sentiment was echoed by Kenneth Johansen, Chief Revenue Officer at Travelport, who added: “As AI takes on a greater role in trip planning, the quality and accuracy of information behind those recommendations will become increasingly important.”

On the other hand, in instances where travellers are struck by cancelled flights, missed connections and sudden changes of plans, rather than queuing at an airport desk or staying on hold for customer service, travellers will get answers in minutes from AI.

"In 2027, servicing will be where travellers truly feel the impact of AI," Niklas Andréen, Chief Commercial Officer, Airline Tech at Sabre Corporation, said.

“Travellers will have disruptions spotted, rebooking options presented and changes confirmed in minutes, often before they've even realised there's a problem. We'll see agents increasingly able to shop, book, rebook and service travel, turning AI from an inspiration tool into a meaningful new distribution and servicing layer for the industry.”

A year after Trump stalled a global net-zero shipping deal, the IMO is trying again – with wind power, batteries, e-fuels and LNG in the mix.

Last year, the Trump administration derailed a global breakthrough aimed at cleaning up shipping, one of the world’s most difficult-to-decarbonise sectors. Now the International Maritime Organization (IMO) is trying again.

Between 23 November and 4 December, the UN agency will meet to discuss the sector’s future Net-Zero Framework. The decisions made will lock in the emissions profile of ships for the next 20+ years.

A framework including a global fuel standard and a pricing mechanism on greenhouse gas emissions from ships was already approved by IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee in spring 2025. It was scheduled for formal adoption in October 2025 – until the POTUS threatened to impose tariffs on all countries that supported it, leading further talks and decision-making to be postponed by a year.

Is there a fresh chance to get a global deal on shipping by the end of 2026? Could the Democrats’ recent victory in the midterm elections offer new momentum? Or will the Net-Zero Framework run aground once and for all?

‘Shipping is one of the hardest to abate sectors’

Euronews Earth spoke to stakeholders working towards deep decarbonisation of the sector. While they anticipate stormy weather along the course, there are also a few glimmers of hope on the more distant horizon.

Shipping moves more than 80 per cent of global trade by volume and is responsible for 2.3 per cent of global CO2 emissions, roughly the same as the entire annual emissions of Japan. Promising solutions already exist, but scaling them depends on infrastructure, investment and policy frameworks.

“Shipping is one of the hardest to abate sectors”, says Dr Peter Schniering, CEO and co-founder of Future Cleantech Architects (FCA), a science-based non-profit organisation and innovation think tank headquartered in Germany. His colleague, FCA Cleantech Analyst Pauline Leroi, provided much of the data and analysis below.

About 90 per cent of the global shipping fleet runs on oil-based fuels. Tankers, container ships and bulk carriers are “the biggest polluters”, says Leroi, followed by cruise ships and general cargo ships. Together, those five vessel types are responsible for 664 million tonnes of CO2 emissions per year. Europe is responsible for 14 per cent of those shipping emissions (China 17 per cent, USA 9 per cent).

The majority of emissions come from large deep-sea shipping vessels. There are currently around 6,000 container ships sailing the world’s oceans and rivers, 8,200 oil tankers, some 13,000 bulk carriers and 960 ships used for tourism.

Wind assisted propulsion and onboard carbon capture: Tools for net-zero shipping

Leroi unpacks the different pathways to net-zero shipping, from alternative fuels to electrification and efficiency solutions, and explains the trade-offs behind them. Slow steaming would be an efficient first step, in her opinion, especially for container ships: “Steaming 10 per cent slower results in up to 20 per cent less fuel burnt.”

There is no magic nautical treasure map – it looks more like a jigsaw puzzle, combining several solutions that fit well together. “Efficiency improvements – such as better hydrodynamics, smarter logistics, upgraded machinery, digitalisation – can save five to 20 per cent of greenhouse gas emissions,” says Leroi. “Wind assisted propulsion systems and on-board carbon capture could save up to a further 25 per cent of GHG emissions.”

Wind-power assisted propulsion systems, such as rotor sails, suction sails or wing sails, could bring down GHG emissions by up to 30 per cent per nautical mile – if weather and wind conditions are favourable. That is mostly the case on busy transatlantic or transpacific routes: “There’s lots of wind around there, usually,” Leroi says.

However, “that’s not the best solution for container ships”, which already have containers piled up, leaving little room for high-towering systems. “But it would be good for tankers and bulk carriers.”

Some 150 ships already have wind assistance today. For tankers, combining wind assistance with shore power, plugging into the port’s electricity supply instead of running onboard generators while docked, could save up to 70 million tonnes of CO2 per year, Leroi says.

“The biggest GHG reduction, however, could come from changing marine fuels – up to 90 per cent reduction, as well as from new propulsion technologies, up to 100 per cent (battery-electric, battery hybridisation, nuclear)”, Leroi says.

Redesigning shipping ports for an electric future

Regarding electric battery solutions, Leroi is in favour and mentions China, which is already operating a 120-metre-long all-electric container vessel on the Yangtze, the world’s third-longest river. “Specifically smaller cargo vessels should all go electric,” she recommends. In a second wave, shorter and medium distance cargo shipping routes could opt for electric battery systems as well.

Smaller cargo vessels should all go electric.

This needs a container battery swapping system at ports along the ship’s route: instead of bunkering oil or gas, cargo ships take onboard a container packed with batteries. Medium distances could get split, with stopovers enabling vessels to change empty container batteries for fully charged ones.

China leads on swappable container battery systems, but there are start-ups in Europe too. Battery swapping for container ships could save another 35 million tonnes of CO2 per year.

Dual fuel ships could switch from LNG to green alternatives in future

Even without a global IMO deal, a transition will go ahead in the shipping sector anyway, experts agree, albeit at a slower pace. That’s where the European Union steps in. “Let’s take ships running on heavy fuel oil,” Leroi explains: “Under FuelEU Maritime Regulation they will not be compliant by 2030 and European vessels will have to transition to lower carbon emitting fuels.”

“Until green fuels are available at scale, transitional fuels could offer only a limited bridging solution,” Leroi emphasises. “Today, liquefied Natural gas (LNG) is the most mature option” – but still far from perfect. While heavy fuel oil has lifecycle emissions of 92 grams of CO2-equivalent per megajoule, LNG still stands at 76g CO2e/MJ, a 25 per cent reduction. Many EU shipowners have opted for it, as it is compliant under the FuelEU Maritime Regulation and other regulations.

The EU’s FuelEU Maritime Regulation is currently the only fully working regulatory framework designed specifically to cut shipping emissions. Patrick Cummins-Tripodi, FCA’s Brussels-based Cleantech Policy Officer, calls the EU’s approach “a strong basis for greening the sector”, but points to the “fact that LNG-powered ships comply with the FuelEU Maritime Regulation”: as a result, “LNG continues to dominate the ship orderbook”.

Why is this an issue? “There is significant methane slip during onboard combustion as well as methane leakage during upstream fuel production and transition, which is not always accounted for,” Leroi warns.

EU shipping methane emissions rose by 30 per cent in 2025. That’s alarming considering that methane is around 80 times more potent at trapping heat than CO2 over a 20-year timeframe. Cummins-Tripodi adds that “methane emission values at the EU and IMO level do not account for the full impact of methane slip, which if updated could penalise the choice of LNG”.

Ships ordered today will operate well beyond 2050, so the order books show what shipowners are betting on. 78 per cent of vessel orders are still for conventional oil propulsion systems – almost 2,200 ships designed to run on fossil fuels. If shipowners move away from oil, they mostly opt for LNG (407 vessels ordered), then methanol (134), according to the 2025 order book.

“It is important to add that many of those ordered ships have a dual fuel design,” Leroi flags. Dual fuel ships designed for running on LNG, ‘grey methanol’ or on ‘grey ammonia’ – produced using fossil fuels – can later switch to ‘green methanol’ or ‘green ammonia’, produced using renewable energy sources.

“Being able to burn those alternative fuels does not mean that they necessarily will – some of those vessel types will continue to burn heavy fuel oil.”

Why can’t shipping rely on biofuels or e-fuels?

Why not just switch to biofuels, with lifecycle emissions of just 21g CO2eq/MJ?

“The main issue with biofuels when decarbonising the shipping sector is that the biofuels feedstock availability simply cannot meet the scale of shipping’s fuel demand. And they are three to four times more expensive,” explains Leroi.

And what about e-fuels, such as e-methanol, e-ammonia or liquid green hydrogen? “They can offer very significant reductions (in terms of GHG emissions) – but e-fuels are even six to seven times more expensive than heavy fuel oil, for instance.”

Leroi is sceptical about e-ammonia: “It is highly toxic to fish and the maritime environment in general.” Even so, she says low-carbon ammonia “could really cut a lot of emissions” on the largest bulk carriers and container ships, if toxicity and handling are addressed. On liquid green hydrogen, she points to “the very low energy density”, meaning more tanks would be required for the same energy output.

E-methanol, on the other hand, has the advantage that the propulsion technology works well and the technology readiness level is high. Its lifecycle emissions are low, just 28g CO2eq/MJ. But it still is prohibitively expensive, for the moment, because production is lagging behind.

Using it on cargo ships could cut up to an estimated 320 million tonnes of CO2 per year. Cruise ships could also be hybridised with low-carbon methanol, biomethanol or e-methanol, for a further 40 million tonnes, and Europe has “real leverage”, as 97 per cent of cruise ships are built here.

Why don’t e-fuel suppliers ramp up production?

Addressing the issues with production isn’t so simple: “Fuel producers need to know that vessels will buy green fuels. Ship owners need to know these fuels to be available before they order new vessels. And ports need to build bunkering infrastructure that connects the two,” Leroi explains.

One of those first movers is Knud Erik Andersen, co-founder and CEO of European Energy, a company in sustainable energy generation. It has invested heavily in battery storage, solar and wind power, and in Power-to-X facilities – plants producing sustainable e-fuels using renewable energy sources.

With the recently inaugurated Kasso site in Denmark, European Energy made headlines. It is the world’s first large-scale commercial e-methanol facility, with an annual production capacity of 42,000 tonnes – and operating entirely on solar energy. The plant, next to Northern Europe’s largest solar park, produces e-methanol with up to a 97 per cent reduced carbon footprint compared to fossil-based products.

“We need long-term regulatory certainty that Europe sticks to these commitments and ambitions,” says Lars Dyrholm, CEO of the Kasso plant. “We have plans for more plants [but] when you make an investment as large as this, you really need certainty for the future income... No one will make an investment like this unless they are sure that the product produced can compete in the market.”

Andersen has a proposal: “Why shouldn’t the public sector in Europe buy e-fuels for naval ships, for the defence industry? The public sector could not only give support by grants and subsidy schemes, it could also act as a customer.”

Measures such as the sustainable maritime fuel allowances under the EU’s Emissions Trading System (ETS) “may help with the final cost, but it may not solve the chicken-and-egg problem” with supply and demand, Cummins-Tripodi says. Incentives and/or tough legal obligations are needed to ensure that all stakeholders take the necessary steps.

An e-fuel market still needs to be created, production needs to be scaled up globally, and the world is still waiting for a reliable international legal framework from the IMO.

Saving 280 tonnes of CO2 each day per ship

One of the biggest buyers of green methanol produced at Kasso is the Danish logistics group Maersk, which is converting part of its global fleet to sustainable fuels.

The world’s first methanol-enabled cargo ship, the 172-metre Laura Maersk, started service in 2023. This was followed in 2024 by Ane Maersk, a 350-metre container vessel carrying up to 16,000 containers when fully loaded. Compared to a sister ship powered by heavy fuel oil, the Ane Maersk saves 280 tonnes of CO2 per day.

Ten more dual-fuel methanol vessels joined the Maersk fleet in 2025, bringing the company’s total to 19 (out of some 700 vessels). The target for 2030 is 94 dual fuel vessels.

Maersk stresses the importance of global regulation – and deeply regrets the delay of adopting the Net-Zero Framework: “Our climate transition plan is significantly dependent on the regulatory landscape, especially our ability to shift to lower greenhouse gas emission fuels,” the company states. “This signature regulatory framework would lay the foundation for closing the price gap between lower GHG emission fuels and fossil-based fuels.”

Port Esbjerg wants to become an international benchmark for sustainability

At Port Esbjerg, where Denmark borders the North Sea, COO Jesper Bank says: “It’s quite clear for us from a strategic perspective that we have to be able to serve a multi-fuel market. But it is also very clear that this path forward is not clear, because you have many [fuelling] alternatives today.”

“The effort from the political side should not be on the technical issues – we will solve that. But it should be on creating the framework, the conditions for the market to develop,” Bank says.

He also calls for European alignment on hydrogen: “We need coordination of national hydrogen strategies. These are very different today: Sweden has one strategy, Denmark doesn’t really have one and Germany has still another one.”

The regulatory gap extends to ports, says Cummins-Tripodi: “Apart from the EU’s Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation’s loose target for LNG, there is no obligation on ports or fuel suppliers to ensure the supply of alternative fuels.”

Uncertainty is increasing pressure on shipowners

Shipowners are adrift in an ocean of regulatory uncertainty. Some in-depth studies, such as classification society DNV’s 10th Maritime Forecast to 2050, alert that “regulatory uncertainty is increasing pressure on shipowners”.

It stresses the urgent need for “stronger global regulatory signals” that “could accelerate the uptake of energy-efficient measures, enabling the global fleet to consume up to 25 per cent less energy by 2050 compared to a scenario where regulation is driven [only] by regions”.

The global Net-Zero Framework

Getting the global Net-Zero Framework adopted would create a pricing mechanism with set prices on the greenhouse gases ships emit, to encourage the industry to lower emissions to comply with a global fuel standard. It would apply to all oceangoing ships over 5,000 gross tonnage – the vessels responsible for over 85 per cent of global shipping emissions – and IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee would set up a Sustainable Fuel Certification Scheme to make sure fuel emissions and sustainability get independently verified.

If the greenhouse gas fuel intensity is too high, a price has to be paid. If a ship emits below a certain threshold or switches to zero or near-zero emission fuels, it will get financially rewarded. IMO could set up a Net Zero Fund, collecting revenue from non-compliant, heavily polluting ships to reward low-emission ships.

It should not really be called a global carbon tax, the IMO insists. It would be more of a performance-based GHG-intensity target system: vessels that exceed pollution limits must pay tiered compliance fees, while those that outperform can earn tradeable credits and be eligible for rewards.

Cummins-Tripodi isn’t optimistic about the talks. “Last year’s proposal will probably not survive,” he says. “It is highly unlikely.”

The IMO deal to some extent mirrors the EU’s approach, including a greenhouse gas intensity reduction target for shipping, but he warns of a shortcoming: “it could be cheaper for companies to pay penalties instead of complying”.

If the IMO route fails, the EU’s FuelEU Maritime Regulation remains the main rulebook for shipping emissions.

Income inequality in the EU fell slightly in 2025. But the gap between rich and poor still varies widely across Europe. Euronews Business takes a closer look at how it is changing and why.

Economic growth only leads to social progress if it is shared fairly, according to Eurostat, the EU’s official statistical office. High inequality damages social cohesion, holds back economic activity and weakens democratic participation.

Is income inequality rising or falling in Europe? Eurostat figures for the EU show a slight decline. In 2025, income inequality in the EU fell to its lowest level in the current series, which begins in 2010. However, this is a relatively short period. Data going further back could give a better picture.

So, where in Europe is income inequality highest? Where is the gap between the rich and the poor widest?

How is income inequality measured?

The Gini coefficient is used to measure income inequality. It compares how income is distributed in a country with a situation where income is shared perfectly equally. It uses disposable household income adjusted for household size and composition.

A value of 0 means perfect equality, where everyone has the same income. A value of 100 means complete inequality, where one person receives all the income.

Turkey and Bulgaria have the highest inequality

According to Eurostat, the Gini coefficient ranges from 23.0 in Slovakia to 43.9 in Turkey across the 34 European countries covered, using the latest available figures. Bulgaria has the highest income inequality in the EU at 37.7, while the EU average is 29.2.

Latvia (35.6), Lithuania (35.5), and Serbia (32.0) complete the top five.

Greece and Montenegro (31.6 each), Cyprus (31.2), and Italy and Switzerland (31.0 each) follow. The figures for Montenegro and Switzerland are from 2024.

Why is income inequality so low in Slovakia and Belgium?

Slovakia has the lowest income inequality, with a Gini coefficient of 23.0. According to a European Commission report, this is due to small differences in incomes before taxes rather than redistribution. However, the report warns that certain groups remain disadvantaged and regional gaps persist.

Belgium (23.4), Norway (23.7), Czechia (24.0), Slovenia (24.6) and Poland (24.9) also have Gini coefficients below 25.

In Belgium, “extensive tax and transfer policies and strong institutionalised social dialogue” help keep income inequality low, according to the OECD.

Among the EU’s major economies, Germany (30.1), France (30.4), Spain (30.8) and Italy (31.0) are all above the EU average.

Among the Nordic countries, Norway is still one of the most equal. However, Denmark (28.2) and Sweden (28.6) now have higher inequality than Poland (24.9) and Romania (27.3). Finland (27.1) is just below Romania.

Why does inequality vary so much?

Income inequality varies greatly across countries because it is shaped by a range of local factors, according to Francisco J. Delgado, associate professor at the University of Oviedo in Spain. He points to the labour market, unemployment, wages and government policy.

“The labor market institutions, the redistributive capacity of taxes and transfers, the economic structure and productivity, and the human capital and equal opportunity are key drivers behind income inequality,” he told Euronews Business.

Why does Bulgaria still have the EU’s highest inequality?

Bulgaria continues to record the highest inequality in the EU. Its 2025 level (37.7) is slightly above its 15-year average (37.4). Delgado said “this divergence stems from a combination of factors.”

The first is regressive taxation, with a flat personal income tax combined with high indirect taxes. The second is weak social transfers, including pensions and social assistance. He also points to a divided labour market with a large informal economy, and to deep demographic and regional gaps, with Bulgaria leading economic growth.

According to the OECD, Bulgaria’s high inequality comes from large gaps in market incomes combined with weak redistribution. Its flat 10% income tax, with no individual tax-free allowance, is one reason the system does little to reduce inequality.

Slight decline in the EU since 2010

In 2025, the EU’s Gini coefficient fell slightly to 29.2, down from 29.4 in 2024. This is the lowest level in the current EU series, which begins in 2010.

Comparing the latest figures with the average of the available data from 2010–2024 shows how far current levels are above or below their historical averages. The EU’s Gini coefficient was 29.2 in 2025, compared with an average of 30.2 over the previous 15 years.

Romania and Poland are furthest below their past averages in the EU

Romania is furthest below its past average. Its Gini coefficient was 27.3 in 2025, 6.4 points below its average (33.7).

North Macedonia (−4.7), Poland (−4.0), Serbia (−3.5) and Montenegro (−2.9) also stand well below their past averages. Among EU countries, Spain (−2.5), Portugal (−2.3) and Belgium (−2.2) follow Poland.

Delgado said the trend in Poland and Romania has been driven mainly by robust economic growth, though the two countries differ.

Between 2015 and 2025, GDP per capita adjusted for purchasing power rose from 70% to 81% of the EU average in Poland and from 56% to 78% in Romania, he said. He also pointed to sharp increases in the minimum wage, especially in Poland, as well as the expansion of the welfare state and EU funding.

Inequality is above past averages in Hungary and several Nordic countries

Inequality rose most in Hungary. Its Gini coefficient was 29.5 in 2025, 1.9 points above its average of 27.6.

Sweden (+1.6) and Finland (+1.3) follow. Switzerland (+1.0), Turkey (+0.9) and Luxembourg (+0.9) also recorded higher levels in their latest figures. Denmark was 0.8 points above its average, while Norway was 0.8 points below.

Delgado said the Nordic countries have faced economic difficulties in recent years, with high unemployment in Finland and Sweden.

Turkey stays well above the EU average

Turkey’s Gini coefficient has stayed at around the same level since 2010. In 2025, it was 43.9, compared with a 2010–2024 average of 43. In 2025, the gap between Turkey and the EU was nearly 15 points.

High income inequality in Turkey reflects large gaps in education, skills and earning capacity, according to the OECD. “The tax and benefit system is among the least redistributive in the OECD, because it is narrow,” its 2025 report says.

In many countries, the latest figures are close to their past averages. Austria and Lithuania are only 0.1 points below their averages, while Malta is 0.1 points above.

From chasing the Northern Lights in Swedish Lapland to exploring Europe’s best Christmas markets or taking a festive train journey, here’s what to see and where to go this December.

December is one of the busiest months in the travel calendar, but there are plenty of reasons to get away beyond the traditional festive city break.

From chasing winter sun in Madeira to seeing the Northern Lights in Scandinavia, the final month of the year offers everything from outdoor adventures to festive cultural events.

Europe’s cities are also getting into the Christmas spirit, with markets, light festivals and seasonal attractions in full swing.

Here’s where to go, what to see and what to book in Europe in December 2026.

Destinations

Lapland, Sweden

December is a particularly atmospheric time to visit Swedish Lapland, where snow-covered forests, frozen lakes and long polar nights create the setting for a classic winter escape. Jukkasjärvi, near Kiruna, is home to the Icehotel, which opens its seasonal ice rooms on 11 December.

Founded in 1989, the hotel is rebuilt every winter using blocks of pure ice harvested from the adjacent Torne River.

The surrounding region is also a good base for husky sledging and snowmobiling, and literally walking in a winter wonderland.

You’re also most likely to spot the Northern Lights here in December, as the time of year offers some of the longest and darkest nights of the year due to the polar night.

Madeira, Portugal

Madeira is a strong choice for anyone looking to swap grey skies for milder weather without travelling too far from mainland Europe.

The Portuguese island has a busy festive programme throughout December, with Funchal’s streets and waterfront illuminated for Christmas and a calendar of seasonal events running into the New Year.

The island’s biggest spectacle comes on 31 December, when fireworks light up the bay of Funchal. It’s one of the best-known New Year’s Eve displays in all of Europe – and for very good reason.

Events and attractions

Amsterdam Light Festival, Netherlands

Amsterdam’s canals become an open-air gallery during the annual Light Festival, with illuminated artworks installed around the city.

From its launch on 26 November, the best way to see the displays is by walking along the waterways or taking a dedicated boat tour, which offers a different perspective on the installations.

The festival runs until 17 January 2027, so there’s time to visit after the Christmas rush.

Fête de l’Escalade, Geneva, Switzerland

From 11-13 December, Geneva marks one of the most important episodes in its history with three days of costumed processions, music and traditional food. The Fête de l’Escalade commemorates the city’s defence against an attempted attack by the Duke of Savoy’s troops in 1602.

The Old Town becomes the focus of the celebrations, with historical demonstrations, lantern processions and a large parade on the Sunday. Look out for the traditional chocolate cauldrons, which are smashed and shared as part of the festivities.

Tivoli Gardens, Copenhagen

Christmas comes early at the Tivoli Gardens in Copenhagen – well, sort of. Running from 13 November to 3 January 2027, the Danish capital’s amusement park takes on a festive makeover for Christmas, with illuminated trees, decorations, seasonal food stalls and plenty of rides.

Christmas markets

December is, obviously, the best time to head to one of Europe’s countless Christmas markets to eat, drink and shop for gifts. These are some of the best to visit this festive season.

Strasbourg, France

Calling itself the “Christmas market capital”, Strasbourg has been hosting its market since 1570. Running from 27 November to 24 December, the city’s historic centre is filled with wooden chalets selling decorations, gifts and Alsatian food, while the enormous Christmas tree in Place Kléber is an absolute must-see.

Dresden, Germany

Dresden’s Striezelmarkt dates back to 1434 and is one of Germany’s oldest Christmas markets. The 592nd edition of the market runs from 25 November to 24 December and is particularly known for its traditional crafts, wooden decorations and Stollen, the rich fruit bread that is a festive speciality of the region.

Prague, Czechia

The majority of Christmas markets close for business in December, but Prague’s runs from 28 November to 6 January 2027, meaning you can head there for a pick-up after the Christmas hubbub has died down. The Czech capital’s Old Town Square provides a spectacular setting for its Christmas market, with the Gothic and Baroque architecture forming a backdrop to the stalls and enormous tree. Wenceslas Square also hosts a market which is well worth a visit.

Tallinn, Estonia

Known as an increasingly cool city to visit, Tallinn at Christmas is pretty special too. Running from 20 November to 6 January 2027, the Estonian capital’s market takes place in the medieval Town Hall Square, where wooden stalls sit beneath the spires and pastel-coloured buildings of the Old Town. A large Christmas tree stands at its centre, surrounded by stalls selling Estonian handicrafts, festive decorations and local food. Expect warming winter dishes, gingerbread and plenty of glögi, the local take on mulled wine.

Festive rail journeys

The Santa Claus Express, Finland

For a festive journey with a real sense of occasion, the Santa Claus Express takes passengers from Helsinki or Turku north into Finnish Lapland, travelling overnight through forests, frozen lakes and snow-covered countryside to the Arctic Circle.

There’s even the chance of spotting the Northern Lights along the way.

Wake up in Rovaniemi, officially known as the hometown of Santa Claus and located on the Arctic Circle. The obvious first stop is Santa Claus Village, where visitors can meet Father Christmas and visit the Santa Claus Main Post Office to send letters and postcards bearing a special Arctic Circle postmark.

The double-decker night train offers seating carriages and sleeper cabins, including deluxe options with private bathrooms and showers. There’s also a dining car serving breakfast, meals and snacks.

Cogwheel train to Santa’s House, Switzerland

This festive trip starts in Montreux, where a cogwheel railway climbs for 55 minutes to Rochers-de-Naye, more than 2,000 metres above sea level.

The journey offers sweeping views across Lake Geneva and the Swiss Alps, before arriving at Santa’s House at the summit. Children can meet Santa and have their photograph taken with him.

Special services run on selected dates from 20 November to 24 December, with combined tickets covering the return journey and entry to Santa’s House.

La Dolce Vita Orient Express ‘Jingle Route’

For a luxury option, the La Dolce Vita Orient Express is running a three-day, two-night trip from Rome to Venice and Florence, departing on 19 December.

The “Jingle Route” journey includes a private boat transfer through Venice’s canals to the Orient Express Venezia hotel for dinner and live music, followed by an afternoon exploring Florence the next day.

Passengers return to the train for dinner and entertainment before arriving back in Rome the following morning. Prices start from €6,560 per person.

New Year’s Eve

If you are planning to see in 2027 away from home, several major cities offer large-scale celebrations, with fireworks, street parties and public events drawing crowds from around the world.

London’s fireworks over the River Thames are among the best-known, with the display centred on the London Eye and Big Ben – and everyone should see them once in their lives.

Paris traditionally celebrates around the Champs-Élysées and Arc de Triomphe, with a countdown and light show drawing crowds to the city centre.

In Madrid, revellers gather at Puerta del Sol to eat the traditional 12 grapes at midnight, one for each stroke of the clock. This unique experience is rounded off with cheers, people using noise-makers, and plenty of toasts using – what else? – Spanish cava.

Edinburgh’s Hogmanay is arguably the most legendary New Year’s Eve event in Europe. Its programme of street celebrations and music culminates in fireworks above the castle and, of course, choruses of Robert Burns’ “Auld Lang Syne” set to music.

Planning ahead for 2027 travel

If you’re already thinking about where to travel next year, December is a good time to start looking beyond the usual holiday hotspots. Luckily, plenty of industry reports have highlighted destinations expected to attract more visitors in 2027, and Euronews Travel’s team has even made predictions.

Smaller European cities, lesser-known islands and countries offering alternatives to established favourites are all set to make a splash in 2027.

Italy remains enormously popular but, if you want to experience a more authentic side of the country, plump for Perugia, with its medieval streets, food scene and annual jazz and chocolate festivals, or Pescara on the Adriatic coast.

Reims in France, Bratislava in Slovakia, Šibenik in Croatia, León in Spain and the Swedish twin coastal towns of Skanör-Falsterbo are also set to be popular, relatively under-the-radar destinations for the upcoming year, while Albania will likely see its popularity rise even further.

Our own predictions for places further afield include growing interest in China, where expanded visa-free access is making it easier for international visitors to explore, and Indonesian destinations beyond Bali, including Komodo National Park, Lombok and Raja Ampat.

Closer to home, a total solar eclipse on 2 August 2027 will pass over southern Spain and North Africa, with cities including Cádiz, Málaga and Marbella well placed for travellers hoping to see it. Be sure to book accommodation in popular viewing areas well ahead of time.

There is also likely to be more interest in slower, less tightly planned holidays, with travellers looking for longer stays, wellness retreats and places where they can escape the crowds. If you want to get ahead of the rush, now is a good time to start comparing flights and accommodation.

The US's top intelligence official has cautioned that Americans should brace for more technology breakdowns, as a software fault at Delta Air Lines' Atlanta base left more than 1,000 flights running late on Sunday.

The warning comes as Americans face a growing run of failures affecting air travel, Microsoft email services, major banks and the National Security Agency's network.

Weight-check software fails days before Thanksgiving rush

Sunday's fault struck the software Delta uses to check that each aircraft is loaded within safe weight limits. With the Thanksgiving rush only days away, staff fell back on manual procedures to dispatch planes while engineers worked on a fix.

Later in the day Delta said the tool was back online, but its schedule was still disrupted, and it hoped to clear the backlog before nightfall.

The Federal Aviation Administration briefly held some flights heading to Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson airport, one of the busiest in the world and Delta's main base, for roughly an hour.

Keeping a plane within its weight and balance limits is a core safety requirement, an FAA document says, because overloading can weaken the aircraft's structure.

Armenian paediatric oncologist Gevorg Tamamyan told Euronews he is campaigning to lead the WHO with a focus on equity, restoring trust and bringing an outsider's perspective to the organisation.

After a decade at the helm of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus will step down in August 2027.

Now, the international health organisation has to choose his successor at a moment when global health and international cooperation are increasingly fraught.

Seven candidates, each nominated by a different country, are competing to lead the UN health agency. The WHO’s Executive Board will narrow the field to its top three candidates by early February, and the WHO’s next leader will be selected at the World Health Assembly in May 2027.

At 39, Gevorg Tamamyan, an Armenian paediatric oncologist, is the youngest contender for the WHO's top job.

Nominated by Botswana, Tamamyan is also the only candidate who has never held a position within the United Nations. He is positioning himself as an outsider who could bring a fresh perspective to the organisation.

“I'm coming kind of outside of the box. I'm coming with different experience,” he told Euronews from Geneva, where the WHO Candidate Forum took place this week.

As a working doctor, he says he had to translate WHO guidance from decree to the clinic, where "the consequences, or the failure, had real consequences for the actual people, actual patients, actual families”.

He argued his outsider perspective will be particularly important because people working within an organisation can sometimes struggle to see its shortcomings.

His career spans clinical practice, the development of national health systems, global diplomacy and humanitarian work in conflict zones.

“Throughout my career, I have observed that there are things which can be done much better, which affect people's lives, and I saw that WHO has most of the tools to make that happen,” Tamamyan said.

He is campaigning under the slogan “Geography must not decide who lives.” He said his commitment to equal access to health was rooted in his own experience of coming from a small, lower-middle-income country, and that it had shaped his career.

"Human is human. It doesn't matter where they come from," Tamamyan said, arguing that equity should be central to the global health infrastructure.

That principle is central to the WHO leaders' race as the organisation faces growing questions about its role, effectiveness and ability to maintain international cooperation.

New era for global health

The challenges facing the next WHO director-general extend beyond improving the organisation's work, with the agency also facing a crisis of confidence among some of its biggest member states.

In 2026, the United States, the organisation’s biggest historical donor, officially withdrew from the WHO. Argentina has also announced its withdrawal.

At the World Economic Forum in Davos earlier this year, Tedros said that the first two decades of this century were a golden age for global health, but that this period had now come to an end.

If elected, Tamamyan has pledged to visit the U.S. and Argentina during his first 100 days in office, in an attempt to bring them back to the table.

“We are stronger when we are united, and even if we disagree on things, we need to keep everyone at the table. The disagreement in the discussion is better than having no discussion,” he said.

Both countries have criticised the WHO's transparency and its handling of the COVID-19 pandemic. They have also pointed to what they described as "serious structural and operational shortcomings that undermined global trust and highlighted the urgent need for independent, science-based leadership in global health".

Tamamyan acknowledged that underlying problems in the organisation must be addressed to restore trust and accountability.

“We are standing on the shoulders of giants, and there has been a huge, huge progress made in the health care field and medical field within these decades,” he said, adding that "it's always easy to criticise retrospectively”.

It is important to understand how to ensure that the WHO stands firmly on its feet as a leader in global health, Tamamyan said.
